children.label: Ear anatomy: 3 main regions
children: External ear: auricle (pinna), external auditory canal, tympanic membrane (ear drum)
Middle ear: auditory ossicles, oval window, eustachian tube
Inner ear: semicircular canals, vestibule, cochlea
Middle ear: cleft or space like a box, air filled; eustachian tube connects it to the back of the nose
Inner ear: hearing system (cochlea) and balance system (vestibule and semicircular canals)

children.label: External ear: auricle (pinna)
children: External ear has 3 parts: auricle (pinna), external auditory canal, tympanic membrane
Auricle function: to collect sound waves
A flap of elastic cartilage, covered by skin
Rim of the auricle is called the helix
Inferior portion is the lobule, devoid of cartilage
Opens into the external auditory canal

children.label: Auricle: nerve supply
children: Supplied by multiple nerves
Auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3)
CN VII (facial nerve)
CN X (vagus nerve)
Greater auricular nerve (C2,3)
Lesser occipital nerve (C2)
Doctor's note: multiple nerves supply the auricle and also other places, so the most common cause of ear pain is referred pain from adjacent structures
Doctor's note: cervical disc prolapse, dental pain and neck muscle spasm may present with ear pain
Clinical pearl: during ear suction some patients cough due to vagus nerve irritation
Clinical pearl: a branch of the vagus (Arnold's nerve) supplies the posterior part of the ear canal

children.label: Auricle: two diseases
children: Perichondritis: inflammation or infection of the perichondrium (covers the ear cartilage); lobule spared
Cellulitis: infection of the external skin of the auricle; lobule involved

children.label: External auditory canal
children: Measures about 24 mm; extends from the auricle to the tympanic membrane
Divided into 2 parts: cartilaginous and bony
Outer one-third (8 mm) is cartilaginous; inner two-thirds (16 mm) are bony
Skin of the cartilaginous canal is thick and contains ceruminous and pilosebaceous glands that secrete wax

children.label: Ear wax
children: Doctor's note: ear wax = secretions of the ear canal + stem cells + some bacterial elements
Doctor's note: normally the ear cleans itself of wax by movement of the cartilaginous part while moving the jaw
Doctor's note: common mistake is using ear buds; they push wax into the bony part of the canal, where it gets stuck (wax impaction) and the ear cannot expel it
Clarification: the lecture lists 'stem cells' as a component of wax; ear wax is generally described as glandular secretions mixed with shed (desquamated) skin cells and debris

children.label: Tympanic membrane (TM)
children: Dimensions: 9-10 mm height and 8-9 mm width; 0.1 mm thick
Positioned obliquely: forms an angle of 55° with the deep external auditory canal
Two parts: pars tensa and pars flaccida
Three layers: outer epithelial layer (ectoderm)
Middle fibrous layer (mesoderm)
Inner mucosal layer (endoderm)

children.label: TM: left or right
children: Clinical pearl: if the cone of light or the lateral process of the malleus is on the right side, it is the right TM
Clinical pearl: if they are on the left side, it is the left TM
Clarification: cone of light points antero-inferiorly; about 5 o'clock in the right ear and 7 o'clock in the left ear

children.label: Ear examination findings
children: Ear canal: patent or obstructed; any signs of inflammation
Secretions: presence, type and characteristics
TM colour: normal is pearly white or pearly grey
TM colour: red may indicate inflammation or infection
TM colour: yellowish may indicate fluid behind the TM (middle ear effusion)
TM integrity: intact or perforated; if perforated, describe size (small, medium or large)
TM position: normal, retracted toward the inner ear, or bulging toward the external ear
Normal features: cone of light (reflection of otoscopic light) normally at 5 o'clock in right ear and 7 o'clock in left ear
Normal features: lateral process of the malleus; assess its presence and position to identify the side of the TM
Exam pearl, model answer: 'I examined the right ear. The ear canal is patent, with no signs of inflammation or secretions.'

Exam pearl, model answer (cont.): 'The tympanic membrane is in a normal position, with a normal pearly white or pearly grey colour. It is intact, with no perforation. The cone of light and the handle of the malleus are clearly visible.'

children.label: Middle ear: overview and parts
children: Small, air-filled cavity in the temporal bone, lined by epithelium
Separated from the external ear by the TM, and from the inner ear by the oval window
Divided into 3 parts relative to the level of the pars tensa
Epitympanum (attic): above the level of pars tensa
Mesotympanum: at the level of pars tensa
Hypotympanum: below the level of pars tensa
Hypotympanum is connected to the back of the nose by the eustachian tube

children.label: Middle ear: ossicles and windows
children: Auditory ossicles: smallest three bones of the body, connected by synovial joints
Ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes
Clinical pearl: stapes is the smallest bone in the human body
Oval window: responsible for sound transmission; membrane-covered opening connecting middle ear to the vestibule of the inner ear
Round window: responsible for pressure release

children.label: Middle ear: eustachian tube
children: Consists of bone and hyaline cartilage; in contrast to the ear canal, it is 2/3 cartilage and 1/3 bone
Runs from the middle ear to the nasopharynx; normally closed at the pharyngeal end
Opens during swallowing, chewing and yawning
Helps maintain equal pressure on both sides of the ear drum

children.label: Mastoid cavity
children: Bone cavity with pneumatized air cells connected to the middle ear
Air-filled cavity that connects to the epitympanic (attic) part of the middle ear
Part of the temporal bone, which has 4 major parts: petrous, mastoid, squamous and tympanic
Some references consider the styloid process a separate entity of the temporal bone
Mastoid cavity is not part of the middle ear, but connects to it through a passage called the aditus
Clinical pearl: middle ear infection is easily transmitted to the mastoid bone, causing mastoiditis
Clinical pearl: in ear exam, check the area behind the auricle (mastoid area) for signs of inflammation

children.label: Inner ear (labyrinth): overview
children: Also called the labyrinth
2 main divisions: outer bony labyrinth and inner membranous labyrinth
Bony labyrinth: series of cavities in the temporal bone, in three regions: semicircular canals, vestibule, cochlea
Bony labyrinth: lined with periosteum; contains perilymph
Perilymph is similar to CSF (there is a connection between perilymph and CSF)
Membranous labyrinth: series of sacs and tubes inside the bony labyrinth; two sacs: utricle and saccule
Membranous labyrinth: lined with epithelium; contains endolymph
Endolymph: K+ level is high; K+ generates the auditory signals (important for action potential and nerve signal transmission)
Clarification: besides utricle and saccule, the membranous labyrinth includes the semicircular ducts and cochlear duct, which lie inside the corresponding bony spaces

children.label: Balance and semicircular canals
children: Doctor's note: central part responsible for balance: cerebellum
Doctor's note: peripheral parts: semicircular canals, vestibule, eyes, muscles and nerves
Doctor's note: any defect in one of these causes imbalance or dizziness (dizziness is a general term)
Semicircular canals (SCCs): sense rotational (angular) acceleration of the head
Three canals: anterior (superior), posterior and lateral; on each side the 3 SCCs are orthogonal (90° to each other)
Ampulla: pear-shaped expansion at one end of each SCC near the vestibular opening
Cupula: gelatinous layer within each ampulla, extends to the roof of the ampulla sealing the SCC
Crista ampullaris: sensory element of the SCCs; contains hair cells, which extend into the cupula
Doctor's note: moving the head horizontally makes fluid in the lateral canal move on both sides, sending action potentials to the brain
Doctor's note: this moves the eyes to the side the head is moving to, without any vertigo feeling

children.label: BPPV
children: Clinical pearl: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is one of the most common diseases affecting the semicircular canals
Benign: not a serious condition; usually self-limiting
Paroxysmal: occurs in sudden attacks
Positional: related to head position (triggered by head movement)
Vertigo: sensation of spinning; person feels they or their surroundings are spinning
Pathophysiology: otolithic sacs contain crystals called otoliths (calcium carbonate), essential for sensing static movement and gravity
Pathophysiology: otoliths sometimes become dislodged and fall into a semicircular canal, most commonly the posterior SCC (due to gravity)
Pathophysiology: crystals cause abnormal fluid movement in the canal, so vertigo attacks occur especially when the head moves (signals sent to brain while head is not moving)
Clarification: understanding the pathophysiology helps choose the appropriate diagnostic test and therapeutic (repositioning) manoeuvre

children.label: Vestibule
children: Responsible for static motion of the body (e.g. sitting in a moving car)
Central part: cochlea in front and SCCs behind
Contains the utricle and saccule, which are part of the membranous labyrinth
Utricle: detects horizontal linear acceleration
Saccule: detects vertical linear acceleration and changes in gravity
Walls of the utricle and saccule contain a small thickened region called the macula

children.label: Cochlea
children: Responsible for hearing; snail shape, bony spiral canal
Divided into 3 channels: cochlear duct, scala vestibuli, scala tympani
Scala vestibuli: connected to the oval window
Scala tympani: connected to the round window
Sound waves enter the inner ear through the oval window (scala vestibuli)
Excess sound waves (pressure) exit the inner ear through the round window (scala tympani)

children.label: Physiology of hearing
children: 1. Auricle directs sounds into the external auditory canal; sound waves strike the ear drum and it vibrates
2. Central area of the ear drum is connected to the malleus, which starts to vibrate
2. Vibration transmitted malleus, incus, stapes; sound waves are amplified as they move through the ossicles
3. Stapes moves the membrane of the oval window in and out
4. Oval window movement sets up fluid pressure waves in the perilymph
4. Perilymph moves through the cochlea from scala vestibuli to scala tympani; cilia inside the organ of Corti move, causing action potentials and nerve signals to the brain
5. Vibration is then transmitted to the organ of Corti through the perilymph and endolymph
6. From the organ of Corti, impulses go via the 8th cranial nerve to the auditory centres in the temporal lobe, where the sound is identified

children.label: Temporal bone radiology: CT
children: Axial view: the lateral semicircular canal can be identified; its appearance is known as the 'signet ring sign'
Modality: high-resolution CT (HRCT)
Plane: axial and coronal (thin slices, 0.5-1 mm)
Window: bone window
Contrast: usually non-contrast
Clinical pearl: the facial nerve runs inside the middle ear

children.label: How to check a temporal bone CT image
children: Exam pearl: first check the patient profile
1. Describe the type of scan (CT scan)
2. Describe the site of scan (temporal bone)
3. Comment on the section/view (coronal / axial)
4. In CT there are windows, so comment on which window (here: bone window)
5. Comment on the presence of contrast (without I.V. contrast)
6. Comment on the normal anatomical structures
7. Comment on any pathology
Note: the easiest way to comment is to compare the 2 sides
Note: in CT scan bones are white, soft tissues are grey and air is black

children.label: Audiology: overview and tuning-fork tests
children: Audiology topics: pure tone audiogram (PTA), tympanometry, paediatric hearing tests, objective tests
Clinical pearl: assess a patient with hearing loss by ear exam plus Rinne and Weber tests
Clinical pearl: audiological assessments are normally done by an audiologist
Tuning-fork tests: technique and interpretation (lecturer's note: from the Internal Medicine lectures)
Rinne test (important): place base of vibrating tuning fork on the mastoid process
Rinne: when the patient can no longer hear it, position the arms of the fork near the ear canal
Rinne: if heard again, air conduction is better than bone conduction (normal result)
Rinne: air conduction relies on the auricle and middle ear; normally air conduction lasts longer than bone conduction
Rinne: if bone conduction is greater than air conduction, it suggests conductive deafness
Weber test: place vibrating tuning fork in the midline of the head
Weber: sound should be heard equally in both ears; unequal perception may indicate lateralization of hearing loss

children.label: Pure tone audiogram (PTA): the graph
children: X axis = frequency; human ear detects 20-20 000 Hz (speech frequencies about 150-2000 or 2500 Hz)
Y axis = intensity of sound (dB)
Zero intensity does not mean no sound; it means not all people can hear it (a standard value)
Normal hearing: -10 to 20 dB (red line = 20 dB)
0 dB is the standardised reference level (threshold of hearing)
A negative dB value (e.g. -5 dB) means better-than-reference hearing sensitivity
A person who needs > 20 dB to hear has hearing loss; the greater the threshold (dB), the more severe the loss
Patient sits in an isolated room wearing headphones; audiologist turns on sounds
Patient knocks on the window or presses a button if he hears the sound

children.label: PTA: air and bone conduction, symbols
children: Audiologist starts by assessing air conduction (AC) pathway (through the ear canal)
If AC is normal there is no need to assess bone conduction
If abnormal, assess bone conduction (BC), which bypasses the external and middle ear and stimulates the inner ear directly
Any problem in the external or middle ear can cause conductive hearing loss
AC unmasked: right ○, left ✕
AC masked: right △, left □
BC unmasked: right <, left >
BC masked: right [, left ]

children.label: PTA: masking
children: Example: hearing loss in the left ear, sound given in that ear is heard in the right ear; this is masking (cross-hearing)
Used if the other ear has better hearing
Noise is put into the other ear to stop the contralateral ear hearing the test sound
Masking volume is increased until the threshold of the test ear is not affected by an increase in masking volume
Clarification: a loud tone in the poorer ear can travel through the skull and be heard by the better cochlea (cross-hearing)
Clarification: masking noise in the better ear prevents this so the result truly reflects the test ear

children.label: Types of hearing loss
children: Conductive: interruption in mechanical transmission of sound through the external or middle ear
Sensorineural: interruption of sound transmission within the cochlea, along the auditory pathway to the brain, or within the brain

children.label: Interpreting audiograms
children: How to describe: 'This is a pure tone audiogram of a patient' (state patient profile if available), then describe the thresholds
Normal: hearing threshold within the normal range at all frequencies (-10 to 20 dB)
Conductive loss: air conduction shows hearing loss; bone conduction is in the normal range, so problem is in the external or middle ear
Sensorineural loss: both conduction pathways are impaired at the same level
Mixed loss: both conduction pathways are impaired but there is a gap between air conduction and bone conduction
Clarification: right ear = red ○ (AC) and [ (BC); left ear = blue ✕ (AC) and ] (BC)
Clarification: an air-bone gap means the inner ear conducts normally but sound is not reaching it (conductive component)

children.label: Tympanometry
children: A probe goes inside the ear canal to seal it and sends pressure waves to the tympanic membrane
TM vibrates and sends back response waves to the tympanometer, which measures them, gives a diagram and calculates ear canal volume
Normal ear canal volume 0.5-2 (written 'mm' in the lecture; graph axis is compliance in cm³)
If the diagram shows flat or dome shape, look at the volume
Volume more than 2: there is a perforation
Volume in normal range: there is fluid in the middle ear

children.label: Tympanogram types
children: Type A: normal; normal pressure (-150 to 200)
Type B: no response wave (TM does not move); flat or dome-shaped
Type C: there is a response, but shifted towards negative pressure
A: normal
As: reduced compliance at ambient pressure (otosclerosis); 's' stands for shallow tympanogram, but remember it for stiffness
Ad: increased compliance at ambient pressure (ossicular discontinuity); 'd' stands for deep tympanogram; remember disruption of the ossicular chain
B: flat or dome-shaped (fluid in the middle ear), or TM perforation (lecturer's note)
C: maximum compliance at pressures more than -200 mm H2O (negative pressure in middle ear), e.g. eustachian tube obstruction or early otitis media with effusion

children.label: Paediatric hearing tests
children: Distraction test: > 7 months
Visual reinforcement audiometry: > 9 months
Conditioned response / play audiometry: > 2 years
Pure tone audiogram: > 5 years
Doctor's note: children have special tests because they will not cooperate like adults; some tests are subjective and some objective

children.label: Objective tests
children: Otoacoustic emissions (OAE): probe, like tympanometry, sends electrical signals and detects the response from the cochlea, not from the TM
Auditory brainstem response (ABR): like an EEG, detects waves from the brain stem
Acoustic reflex
Clinical pearl: OAE is a newborn hearing screening test; gives pass or fail only (presence/absence of a response, not severity of hearing loss)
Clinical pearl: if the baby fails, the paediatrician refers to ENT, as the cause may not be a disease; it could be wax obstruction
Clinical pearl: if the canal is blocked with wax, clean it; if clear, do the more accurate advanced assessment (ABR)
Clinical pearl: every newborn should undergo hearing screening for early detection and to avoid delayed treatment, especially in congenital hearing loss

children.label: Degrees of hearing loss (audiogram)
children: Degree of hearing loss is measured by audiogram
Degrees: mild · moderate · (moderately severe) · severe · profound
Profound = dead ear, no element of hearing

children.label: Types of hearing loss
children: Sensorineural: originates from inner ear; problem in the cochlea, the nerve, or higher in the brain
Conductive: interruption of the sound reaching the cochlea
Conductive causes: ear wax, otitis externa, infection of the middle ear, ossicular chain problem
Mixed: combination of sensorineural and conductive

children.label: Causes of hearing loss
children: Conductive: fluid, allergies, foreign objects, ruptured eardrum, impacted ear wax
Sensorineural: aging, ototoxicity, loud noise, blast/explosion, tumours
Both: genetic disease, virus/disease/infection, head trauma

children.label: Management of conductive hearing loss
children: Most conductive HL is managed by medical or surgical means
Removal of canal obstructions: impacted wax, foreign body, osteoma or exostosis, keratotic mass, benign or malignant tumours, meatal atresia
Removal of fluid: myringotomy ± grommet insertion
Removal of mass from middle ear: tympanotomy and removal of small middle ear tumours or cholesteatoma behind an intact tympanic membrane
Stapedectomy: as in otosclerotic fixation of the stapes footplate
Tympanoplasty: repair of perforation, ossicular chain, or both
Hearing aid: where surgery is not possible, is refused, or has failed

children.label: Doctor's notes on treating hearing loss
children: Doctor's note: The first step is to check the cause of hearing loss
Doctor's note: Wax: remove it · Infection: treat it · Perforation: insert a graft into the tympanic membrane (tympanoplasty) · Ossicle: prosthetic ossicle
Doctor's note: Conductive hearing loss is easier to treat than sensorineural; it can be treated medically or surgically
Doctor's note: Once the nerve is damaged in SNHL, especially in chronic cases, the nerve is unable to regain its function

children.label: Management of sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
children: Early detection of SNHL is important: measures can stop its progress, reverse it, or start rehabilitation with hearing aids
Sudden SNHL: treated with oral or intratympanic steroids
Ototoxic drugs: use with care and discontinue if causing hearing loss
Noise-induced hearing loss: prevent by ear protection devices or avoiding noise exposure
Rehabilitation of SNHL: hearing aids and cochlear implant

children.label: Cochlear implant (doctor's notes)
children: Doctor's note: The only option is a hearing aid (amplifies the sound so the patient can hear properly)
Doctor's note: Last chance for severe–profound SNHL is the cochlear implant (one of the revolutions in medicine and surgery)
Doctor's note: External receiver (as in a hearing aid) transmits sound to the internal device
Doctor's note: Internally, electrodes inserted inside the cochlea stimulate the spiral ganglion and the nerve, giving an electrical signal to the brain
Doctor's note: A completely implantable cochlear implant (under the skin) is a new development, still under investigation

children.label: Peripheral vestibular disorders
children: Four disorders: Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) · benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) · vestibular neuronitis · labyrinthitis
Doctor's note: Peripheral vestibular disease → balance problem
Doctor's note: Dizziness = general term of imbalance; vertigo = sub-type of dizziness, feeling that the subject or surroundings are spinning or rotating
Doctor's note: Approach to a dizzy patient: (1) which type? (2) central or peripheral? (3) episodic or constant?
Doctor's note: Central: CVA, infarction, haemorrhage (more serious)
Doctor's note: Peripheral, episodic: Ménière's disease (attacks) and BPPV (without Ménière's-like symptoms)
Doctor's note: Peripheral, constant: vestibular neuronitis (no hearing loss) and labyrinthitis (hearing loss)

children.label: Ménière's disease
children: Characterized by vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and sense of pressure in the involved ear
Vertigo of sudden onset; lasts from a few minutes to 24 h
Treatment: low-salt diet · avoid stress, caffeine, cheese and alcohol · intratympanic steroid in acute attacks
Risk factors: young females, high caffeine intake, stress
Pathophysiology: increased pressure of the inner ear fluid triggers the attack; once pressure is relieved, the attack resolves

children.label: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
children: Vertigo when head is placed in a certain critical position; no hearing loss or other neurologic symptoms
Dix–Hallpike test establishes the diagnosis and differentiates it from positional vertigo of central origin
Dix–Hallpike: rotate head backward and toward tested ear to move otoliths (crystals) within semicircular canal, triggering vertigo
Positive test: patient exhibits nystagmus; if positive, Epley manoeuvre can be performed to treat the attack
Caused mainly by disorder of the posterior semicircular canal; many patients have history of head trauma and ear infection
Treated by Epley manoeuvre
Attacks last seconds, much shorter than those in Ménière's disease

children.label: Vestibular neuronitis
children: Severe vertigo of sudden onset with no cochlear symptoms (no hearing loss)
Attacks may last from a few days to 2 or 3 weeks
Thought to be due to a virus attacking the vestibular ganglion
Acute attack managed similar to Ménière's disease (steroids, vestibular suppressants); usually self-limiting

children.label: Labyrinthitis
children: Inflammation of the labyrinth
Symptoms similar to vestibular neuronitis in addition to hearing loss
May be viral or bacterial

children.label: Comparison of peripheral vestibular disorders
children: Ménière's disease: episodic; fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, pressure; few minutes–24 h; ↑ inner-ear fluid pressure; low salt, avoid triggers, intratympanic steroid
BPPV: episodic (seconds); no hearing symptoms; posterior SCC, Dix–Hallpike; treat with Epley manoeuvre
Vestibular neuronitis: constant; no hearing symptoms; days–3 weeks; virus on vestibular ganglion; steroids, vestibular suppressants
Labyrinthitis: constant; hearing loss; viral or bacterial; treatment as neuronitis

children.label: Diseases of the external ear: overview and otitis externa
children: External ear disease groups: congenital disorders · trauma · inflammation · tumours · miscellaneous conditions
Otitis externa, bacterial: localized otitis externa (furuncle) · diffuse otitis externa · malignant otitis externa
Otitis externa, fungal: otomycosis
Otitis externa, viral: herpes zoster oticus · otitis externa haemorrhagica
Features: ear discharge, pain, hearing loss and itchiness
Commonest organisms: P. aeruginosa (swimmer's ear), S. aureus, Candida albicans, Aspergillus niger
Treatment: topical antibiotics, antifungal or antiviral · aural toilet (cleaning ear canal to reduce load of infection) · pain killers

children.label: Bacterial vs fungal otitis externa
children: Bacterial, typical finding: secretion in the ear canal; pus; inflamed pink colour
Fungal, typical finding: hyphae; black spores
Bacterial symptoms: severe pain, purulent discharge
Fungal symptoms: itching
Both: hearing loss, obstruction of the ear canal

children.label: Necrotizing otitis externa
children: Osteomyelitis of the temporal bone (infection reaches temporal bone); severe otitis externa complicated by osteomyelitis
Pain +++, unresponsive to treatment, cranial nerve palsies
Risk groups: diabetics, immunocompromised, elderly
Treated with long-term IV antibiotics (6–8 weeks)
Diagnosis by CT scan: infection causes erosion of the cortical bone of the mastoid

children.label: Perichondritis
children: Infection or inflammation of the auricular cartilage
Causes: auricular cellulitis, herpes zoster, allergic reaction, autoimmune disease (e.g. relapsing polychondritis), post-trauma (e.g. ear piercing, surgery, wrestling), otitis externa
Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (most common, 70%), Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus
Risk of cauliflower ear from fibrocartilage injury if not treated aggressively
Signs: tender, erythematous, warm, oedematous auricle; reduced definition of auricular folds; occasional fever, cervical adenopathy
Pure perichondritis spares the lobule
Treatment: aggressive systemic anti-Pseudomonal antibiotics; steroid therapy if presumed autoimmune

children.label: Two common infections of the auricle
children: Perichondritis: limited to the auricle, sparing the lobule (devoid of cartilage); Pseudomonas
Cellulitis: involves the auricle and lobule (superficial); Streptococcus

children.label: Diseases of the tympanic membrane
children: Retraction of the TM: 4 grades
Myringosclerosis (scarring of the TM)
Perforation

children.label: Diseases of the middle ear: overview
children: Acute otitis media (AOM)
Otitis media with effusion (OME)
Chronic otitis media (COM)
Otosclerosis

children.label: Acute otitis media (AOM)
children: Acute inflammation of the middle ear, usually following an upper respiratory infection
Common pathogens in children: Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
Symptoms: otalgia, fever, decreased hearing
Otoscopy: erythematous, bulging TM; ear canal clean, no secretions or discharge
Pathophysiology: retrograde spread of microorganisms from nasopharynx (throat or sinuses) to middle ear via the Eustachian tube

children.label: AOM management and complications
children: Doctor's note: Management: provide adequate analgesia
Doctor's note: Consider observation, a back-up prescription, or immediate antibiotics according to age, severity, otorrhea, risk factors and local guidance
Doctor's note: Antibiotics are not automatic for every child with AOM (local guidance, age, severity, otorrhea, comorbidity, follow-up reliability)
Doctor's note: Safety-net: reassess if symptoms worsen rapidly, child becomes systemically unwell, or symptoms fail to begin improving within about 3 days
Extra-cranial complications: mastoiditis · facial nerve palsy · bacterial labyrinthitis/vestibulitis · petrositis · temporal abscess
Intracranial complications: meningitis/encephalitis · sigmoid sinus thrombosis · intracranial abscess

children.label: Otitis media with effusion (OME)
children: Insidious condition: accumulation of non-purulent effusion in the middle ear cleft; often thick and viscid, sometimes thin and serous; fluid is nearly sterile
Commonly seen in school-going children
Causes: 1. malfunctioning of the eustachian tube (most common) · 2. allergy · 3. unresolved otitis media
More common in children because the eustachian tube is narrow, short and more horizontal
Image: air bubble and fluid – a chronic process; glue ear = fluid behind the TM

children.label: OME management
children: Exam pearl: assess hearing and impact on speech, learning and daily life; hearing testing and tympanometry when indicated
Exam pearl: Do NOT routinely use antibiotics, decongestants, antihistamines, or oral/nasal steroids – even with glue ear
Exam pearl: Consider monitoring/support, autoinflation in suitable children, hearing support, or ENT discussion of grommets for persistent hearing loss affecting daily life
Watchful waiting is the best option: wait 3 to 6 months
Fluid resolves in most cases (about 70%); in about 30% the patient needs intervention (myringotomy, fluid suction, insertion of ventilation tube)
Myringotomy + ventilation tube (grommet) is the intervention when watchful waiting fails

children.label: Chronic otitis media (COM)
children: Long-standing infection of a part or whole of the middle ear cleft, characterized by ear discharge and a permanent perforation
Clinical features: chronic ear discharge · hearing loss · TM perforation · cholesteatoma in the squamous type
Classification: mucosal (active, inactive, healed) vs squamous (retraction pockets, active cholesteatoma)

children.label: Cholesteatoma
children: Presence of squamous-type epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid – 'skin in the wrong place'
An abnormal type of cell leads to painless chronic ear discharge
Classified into: 1. congenital · 2. acquired, primary · 3. acquired, secondary
Treatment: surgical is the mainstay, to get a clean and safe ear
Medical treatment for patients unfit for surgery

children.label: Otosclerosis
children: Oto = ear, sclerosis = stiffness; primary disease of the bony labyrinth
Most often the focus involves the stapes region → stapes fixation and conductive deafness
Symptoms: progressive hearing loss; tinnitus
Signs: normal ear drum · conductive hearing loss (negative Rinne) · Carhart notch on audiogram
Treatment: surgery (stapedectomy); hearing aids
Doctor's note: Autosomal dominant with variable penetrance
Doctor's note: Negative Rinne is mechanical: the stapes does not move to transmit the sound
Doctor's note: Stapedectomy: a prosthesis is put in rather than the stiff stapes
Doctor's note: Hearing aids: amplification, used if there is a contraindication to surgery

children.label: Temporal bone fractures: definition and classification
children: Usually result from blunt head trauma (road traffic accidents, falls)
Traditional classification: longitudinal vs transverse relative to the petrous ridge
Modern classification (anatomical involvement): otic capsule-sparing vs otic capsule-violating
Otic capsule-sparing: lower risk of severe inner-ear injury; conductive HL common
Otic capsule-violating: significantly more severe; inner ear involvement → high risk of SNHL, severe vertigo, facial nerve injury, CSF otorrhea/rhinorrhea due to dural tearing

children.label: Temporal bone fractures: features, investigations, management
children: Clinical features: hemotympanum · bloody or CSF otorrhea · conductive or sensorineural HL · facial nerve palsy · vertigo and nystagmus · Battle sign (postauricular ecchymosis) · associated intracranial injury
Investigations: CT head (intracranial injuries) · HRCT temporal bone (fracture anatomy) · facial nerve examination (document early, repeat serially) · audiometry once stable
Suspected CSF leak: beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein
Management: initial stabilization (ABC + neurological) · urgent ENT and neurosurgical assessment
Facial palsy: early specialist evaluation, especially complete immediate paralysis
CSF leak: observation and specialist management (persistent leaks may need intervention)
Hearing loss: follow-up audiometry and rehabilitation
Avoid ear irrigation and unnecessary instrumentation when fracture/TM injury is suspected
Antibiotics are not routinely indicated solely because of a CSF leak
Complications: permanent hearing loss · facial nerve paralysis · persistent CSF leak and meningitis · labyrinthine injury and persistent vertigo · intracranial complications

children.label: Practical approach to ear symptoms: history and examination
children: Start with the timeline (sudden vs gradual; acute vs recurrent/chronic)
Ask about pain, discharge, hearing change, tinnitus, vertigo, fever, trauma, water exposure, ototoxic medicines
Risk factors that change urgency: diabetes, immunosuppression, previous ear surgery, cochlear implant, facial weakness
Examine both ears; assess mastoid, pinna, cranial nerves, nose/oropharynx when indicated
Document laterality, onset, otoscopy findings, tuning-fork results and the safety-net plan

children.label: Otoscopy findings
children: Normal TM: translucent/pearly grey; malleus and landmarks visible
AOM: bulging, opaque TM with reduced mobility (redness alone is not diagnostic)
OME: dull/retracted membrane, air–fluid level or bubbles; confirm with tympanometry
Retraction pocket or attic crust/debris: consider cholesteatoma (persistent discharge or hearing loss)
Perforation: describe site and size; look for discharge, granulation, and whether the ear is safe to get wet

children.label: Bedside tests and audiogram
children: Whispered voice/finger rub = screening only
Rinne: AC > BC is normal or sensorineural loss; BC ≥ AC suggests conductive loss
Weber: lateralizes to the poorer ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in unilateral SNHL
Pure-tone audiometry: air–bone gap = conductive; elevated air and bone thresholds without a gap = sensorineural
Tympanometry assesses middle-ear function, not hearing thresholds

children.label: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss – do not miss it
children: New hearing loss developing over ≤ 72 hours is an otologic emergency until assessed
Urgently distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss: otoscopy + tuning forks, then urgent audiometry/ENT assessment
Do not delay referral while waiting for routine testing
Guideline option: corticosteroids may be offered within 2 weeks of onset after discussion of risks/benefits and contraindications
Assess for focal neurological signs, bilateral/recurrent episodes, and arrange evaluation for retrocochlear pathology as appropriate

children.label: Red flags and urgent referral
children: Severe persistent otalgia or otorrhea despite appropriate treatment, especially with diabetes/immunosuppression: think necrotizing otitis externa
Postauricular erythema/swelling, protruding pinna, fever or systemic illness: think mastoiditis
Facial weakness, other cranial neuropathy, meningism, severe headache, focal neurological signs: emergency assessment
Sudden hearing loss, significant vertigo with neurological signs, or penetrating trauma: urgent assessment
Persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult, especially with nasal symptoms or neck mass: evaluate for an obstructing lesion

children.label: Chronic otitis media and cholesteatoma: safe vs unsafe ear
children: Ask about duration/character of discharge, hearing change, previous surgery, water exposure, vertigo and facial symptoms
Cholesteatoma clues: attic/posterosuperior retraction pocket, keratin debris, persistent foul discharge, granulation, or progressive conductive loss
Cholesteatoma can erode ossicles and bone and cause facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula, mastoid or intracranial complications
Keep the ear dry and treat active infection as directed, but topical/medical treatment does not eradicate cholesteatoma
Refer to ENT for assessment and surgical planning
CT temporal bone may define bony disease; MRI diffusion-weighted imaging can help in selected cases

children.label: Vertigo: use timing and triggers
children: Brief (seconds) position-triggered episodes with positional nystagmus: BPPV; perform Dix–Hallpike when appropriate
Continuous acute vertigo for days without hearing loss: vestibular neuritis; new hearing loss raises concern for labyrinthine/cochlear involvement or another diagnosis
Recurrent spontaneous episodes with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus or aural fullness: Ménière's disease
Central warning signs: focal neurological deficit, severe gait/truncal ataxia, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, new severe headache → central cause
Doctor's note: HINTS is for trained clinicians assessing a continuous acute vestibular syndrome – not for brief positional dizziness or untrained use

children.label: MCQs
children: Q: A 58-year-old wakes with unilateral hearing loss and a normal-looking ear. Urgent next step? (Think sudden SNHL.) | A: Urgent audiometry/ENT assessment, consider steroids – sudden SNHL
Q: A child has painless hearing difficulty, a dull tympanic membrane and no fever. Diagnosis and likely hearing assessment? (Think OME.) | A: Otitis media with effusion – hearing testing/tympanometry
Q: A patient with diabetes has severe nocturnal ear pain and granulation in the canal. Which dangerous diagnosis must be excluded? | A: Necrotizing otitis externa
Q: Recurrent brief spinning when rolling in bed, no hearing symptoms. Useful bedside test and treatment manoeuvre? | A: BPPV – Dix–Hallpike, Epley manoeuvre

children.label: References
children: Key references (as listed): AAO-HNSF Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update), 2019
NICE NG233 Otitis media with effusion in under 12s, 2023
NICE NG91 Otitis media (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, updated 2022
Use current local antimicrobial pathways and ENT referral protocols; drug choices and thresholds may vary by setting

children: Doctor's note: focused mainly on the CT scan part; did not explain the anatomy in detail and said to study it on your own
Red text in the original = the doctor's own points; 'Added note' = transcript author's clarification

children.label: External nose
children: Upper bony part: nasal bones (articulate with each other in midline), nasal process of frontal bone, frontal process of maxilla
Lower cartilaginous part: hyaline cartilage, may undergo ossification
Cartilages: upper lateral cartilage, major alar cartilage (= lower lateral cartilage), minor alar cartilage
1-4 minor sesamoid cartilages lie between the upper and lower lateral cartilages

children.label: Blood supply of the external nose
children: Primary supply: external carotid artery -> facial artery
Superior labial artery: supplies the columella and the lateral nasal wall
Angular artery: supplies the nasal side wall, nasal tip and nasal dorsum

children.label: Nasal septum
children: Bony part: vomer, perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, maxillary crest, palatine bone (nasal crest)
Cartilaginous part: quadrangular (septal) cartilage

children.label: Complications of septal surgery (septoplasty)
children: Specific complications: septal hematoma, septal perforation, nasal deformity (e.g. saddle nose)
CSF leak: may occur if perpendicular plate of ethmoid is fractured, because it is continuous with the skull base
Anosmia: when tissue at the level of the skull base / olfactory area is removed or damaged
Doctor's note: in septoplasty you may work on the cartilage and the vomer, but do not get close to the perpendicular plate
Clarification: saddle nose results from loss of septal cartilage support (dorsal strut); can follow overresection of cartilage, not only fracture of perpendicular plate

children.label: Lateral nasal wall
children: Carries three turbinates (inferior, middle, superior); under each lies a corresponding space called a meatus
Inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct opens here
Middle meatus: maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoid cells and frontal sinus open through the hiatus semilunaris
Middle ethmoid cells open on the bulla ethmoidalis (middle meatus)
Superior meatus: posterior ethmoid cells
Sphenoethmoidal recess: sphenoid sinus

children.label: Endoscopic image of the nasal cavity
children: Rigid nasal endoscopic view (rhinoscopy) of the left nasal cavity shows septum, inferior turbinate, middle turbinate
Clarification: slide calls this 'posterior rhinoscopic exam (or rigid endoscopy)'; standard term is rigid nasal endoscopy
Doctor's note: the doctor corrected the side on the slide from right to left

children.label: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area)
children: Confluence of vessels on the anterior part of the nasal septum
Arteries anastomosing: septal branch of sphenopalatine artery, branches of anterior ethmoidal artery, greater palatine artery, septal branch of superior labial artery
Little's area is supplied by 4 arteries; the posterior ethmoidal artery is NOT involved
Little's area = the most common site of epistaxis, especially in young patients

children.label: Woodruff's plexus
children: Woodruff's plexus (naso-nasopharyngeal plexus): anastomosis of posterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine and ascending pharyngeal arteries
Site: posterior part of the lateral nasal wall, near the posterior end of the inferior turbinate
In elderly patients epistaxis most commonly arises from this posterior area, mainly because of anticoagulant use

children.label: Management of epistaxis
children: Clinical pearl: management as given on the slide: topical antibiotic ointment (Fusidine), vasoconstriction
Clinical pearl: if not improved within 1 week -> cauterization
Clarification (first aid): sit patient up leaning forward and pinch the soft part of the nose continuously for 10-15 minutes before anything else

children.label: Venous and lymphatic drainage
children: Sphenopalatine vein -> through sphenopalatine foramen -> pterygoid plexus
Ethmoidal veins -> superior ophthalmic vein
Anterior facial vein -> common facial vein -> internal jugular vein; also communicates with cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins
Angular vein drains the external nose -> ophthalmic vein -> cavernous sinus
The venous system of the nose is valveless
Lymph: anterior portion (toward external nose) -> submandibular nodes; posterior portion -> upper deep cervical nodes
Doctor's note: because of this, infection spreads easily from the nose to the intracranial cavity; hence called the danger area of the face

children.label: Nerve supply of the nose
children: Given in the slides as pictures only (not explained in the lecture)
External nose: supratrochlear, infratrochlear, external branch of anterior ethmoidal, infraorbital and external nasal nerves
Nasal cavity: anterior and posterior ethmoidal, septal, nasopalatine and greater palatine nerves
Clarification: general sensation from ophthalmic division V1 (anterior/posterior ethmoidal, infratrochlear, supratrochlear)
Clarification: and from maxillary division V2 (infraorbital, nasopalatine, greater palatine, sphenopalatine branches); smell carried by olfactory nerve (CN I)

children.label: Paranasal sinuses: development
children: Paranasal sinuses: frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary
Maxillary: present at birth; rapid growth from birth to 3 years; adult size at 15 years; first radiologic evidence 4-5 months after birth
Ethmoid: present at birth; adult size by 12 years; first radiologic evidence at 1 year
Frontal: not present at birth; invades frontal bone at 4 years; size increases until the teens; first radiologic evidence at 6 years
Sphenoid: not present at birth; reaches sella turcica by 7 years, dorsum sellae by late teens, basisphenoid in adulthood
Sphenoid: adult size at 15 years; first radiologic evidence at 4 years
Only the ethmoid and maxillary sinuses are present at birth

children.label: Sinus histology and functions
children: Lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells
Nasal cilia beat 10-20 times per second at room temperature
Functions: humidification, vocal resonance, mucus production, absorbing shock to the head, regulation of intranasal pressure

children.label: Arterial supply of the sinuses
children: Frontal: supraorbital artery (ophthalmic <- internal carotid) and anterior ethmoidal artery (ophthalmic artery)
Ethmoid: anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (ophthalmic artery - internal carotid system)
Maxillary: infraorbital artery and anterior/middle/posterior superior alveolar arteries (all from maxillary artery <- external carotid)
Sphenoid: posterior ethmoidal artery (ophthalmic artery) and branches of pharyngeal artery (from maxillary artery)

children.label: Ostiomeatal complex (OMC)
children: Clarification: OMC is the common drainage pathway of maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses at the middle meatus
Components: uncinate process, hiatus semilunaris, ethmoid bulla, infundibulum and maxillary ostium
Clarification: blockage of this narrow area is the key cause of chronic rhinosinusitis, which is why FESS focuses on opening it

children.label: Radiology: views of the CT scan
children: Axial: a horizontal slice, seen from top-down or bottom-up
Sagittal: a side view, from left to right
Coronal: a front-to-back view
Doctor's note: to understand CT scans, remember the views first
Doctor's note: when asked to 'describe this image', start with the type of image (CT, of what? - of the paranasal sinuses), then describe the structures seen and any findings

children.label: High-yield facts: complaints and bones
children: Doctor's note: main patient complaints in ENT clinics: snoring, mouth breathing, nasal obstruction and headache
Doctor's note: one of the most frequently requested investigations in ENT is the CT scan
Inferior turbinate: a separate facial bone, unlike middle and superior turbinates, which are parts of the ethmoid bone
Facial bones = 14: 2 maxillae, 2 zygomatic, 2 nasal, 2 lacrimal, 2 palatine, 2 inferior nasal conchae, 1 vomer, 1 mandible
Cranial bones = 8: 1 frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, 1 occipital, 1 sphenoid, 1 ethmoid

children.label: High-yield facts: turbinates and lamina papyracea
children: Middle turbinate: part of ethmoid; attaches superiorly to the cribriform plate
Cribriform plate: thinnest part of the skull base and most common site of spontaneous CSF leak
Turbinate accidentally fractured in FESS: middle turbinate -> main complication CSF leak (attachment to cribriform plate)
Inferior turbinate fractured: no risk of CSF leak (separate facial bone, not attached to skull base)
Lamina papyracea: thin bony wall between ethmoid sinus and orbit; barrier stopping infection spread from ethmoid to orbit
'Every time I get a cold, my eye swells' = lamina papyracea dehiscence
Similarly 'every time I get otitis media, I develop facial paralysis' = facial nerve canal dehiscence

children.label: CT Image 1: coronal, frontal sinus level
children: Description: coronal CT scan of the paranasal sinuses
Structures seen: right and left frontal sinuses (FS), nasal bone, nasal septum
Doctor's note: there are 2 frontal sinuses - don't say 3; the extra appearance is a septation or a piece of bone coming down into the cut
Doctor's note: may come across unilateral or bilateral frontal aplasia in a patient
Doctor's note: turbinates not shown yet because this cut is still anterior

children.label: CT Image 2: coronal, ethmoid, orbits and maxillary sinuses
children: Doctor's note: this image is very important and always comes in the exam (coronal CT of the paranasal sinuses)
Description: coronal CT of the paranasal sinuses at the level of the ethmoid sinuses and the orbits
Structures: right and left orbit; right and left ethmoid sinus; crista galli; perpendicular plate of ethmoid; cribriform area
Structures: fovea ethmoidalis; lamina papyracea ('paper-like'); Haller cell; uncinate process
Structures: right and left maxillary sinus; right and left middle turbinate; right and left inferior turbinate

children.label: CT Image 2: doctor's points (1)
children: Cribriform area: point of attachment of middle turbinate; most common site of CSF leak; thinnest area of skull base
Anterior vs posterior ethmoid cell: look at attachment of middle turbinate (basal lamella): vertical -> anterior ethmoid cell; horizontal -> posterior ethmoid cell
Lamina papyracea: ethmoid sinus problems can lead to orbital complications because of the thin bone between the two
Haller cell: ethmoid cell that pneumatizes into the roof of maxillary sinus; if larger than normal may block maxillary outflow -> risk factor for maxillary sinusitis
Uncinate process: acts like a valve opening and closing maxillary sinus drainage -> first step in FESS is the uncinectomy

children.label: CT Image 2: doctor's points (2)
children: Facial bones: mandible, vomer, maxilla, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine and inferior nasal conchae
Unilateral clear fluid: patient says fluid comes out of nose when he lowers his head, and it is unilateral -> ddx = CSF leak
Inferior concha fracture is acceptable; never the middle and superior (they originate from ethmoid; fracture -> CSF leak)
Inferior concha is a separate facial bone; in operations for hypertrophied inferior turbinate we may fracture it out so the patient can breathe
Clarification: slide wrote 'perpendicular plate' for the attachment separating anterior from posterior cells; actual separator is basal lamella of the middle turbinate
Clarification: 'Fovia' on the slide = fovea ethmoidalis (roof of the ethmoid)
Mention 3 complications of septoplasty: CSF leak (close to perpendicular plate of ethmoid); saddle nose deformity (also if perpendicular plate is broken)
Septoplasty complications also: septal hematoma and perforation; anosmia

children.label: CT Image 3: coronal, sphenoid sinus, optic nerves, carotids
children: Description: coronal CT at the level of the sphenoid sinus: right and left sphenoid sinuses, optic nerves, both carotid arteries, middle turbinates, inferior turbinates, maxillary sinuses
Notice the close relation between the sphenoid sinus, the optic nerve and the internal carotid artery
Complications of sphenoid sinus surgery: blindness and bleeding from the carotid
Infection spread from sphenoid sinus: thrombophlebitis (cavernous sinus thrombosis); inflammation and compression of structures within or in the wall of the sinus
Clinical pearl: most common sinus related to cranial nerve or optic nerve complications = sphenoid sinus
Clinical pearl: most common sinus related to orbital complications = ethmoid sinus

children.label: Cavernous sinus
children: Venous sinus lateral to the sphenoid sinus, on either side of the pituitary gland
Contains internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, VI, V1 and V2
Several cranial nerves controlling eye movements affected -> ophthalmoplegia (paralysis of eye muscles) = 'frozen eye': eye cannot move in any direction
Clarification: original slide listed the jugular vein among contents; what runs inside is the internal carotid artery (with sympathetic plexus), not the jugular vein

children.label: CT Image 4: coronal, sphenoid sinuses and nasopharynx
children: Description: coronal CT at level of sphenoid sinuses and nasopharynx: right sphenoid sinus, left sphenoid sinus (smaller than the right), air-filled nasopharynx below them
Clinical case (doctor): 70-year-old with nasal obstruction and mouth breathing; CT shows opacification in the nasopharynx (cyan area)
Most likely diagnosis in 70-year-old -> nasopharyngeal cancer
If it were a 3-year-old -> adenoid hypertrophy

children.label: CT Image 5: coronal, posterior sphenoid region
children: Description: coronal CT at the level of posterior sphenoid sinus: right and left sphenoid sinuses, optic nerve, internal carotid artery, foramen rotundum, vidian canal, vomer, inferior turbinates
ON = optic nerve; ICA = internal carotid artery (original slide wrote 'external' and was corrected)
FR = foramen rotundum, on the posterior lateral side; maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve (V2) passes through it
VC = vidian canal, on the posterior inferior side
Vomer = posterior inferior part of the nasal septum
Clarification: letters CP and IOR also on the slide but not explained in lecture (CP likely clinoid process, IOR likely infra-optic recess of sphenoid sinus - to be confirmed)

children.label: CT Image 6: axial, septum, maxillary sinuses, nasopharynx
children: Description: axial CT of paranasal sinuses: nasal septum, right and left maxillary sinuses, inferior turbinates, post-nasal space (nasopharynx)
The axial view is the best view to see septal deviation
The inferior turbinate attaches to the lateral wall of the maxillary bone
Clinical case: 70-year-old with nasal obstruction, snoring, mouth breathing; axial CT shows lesion in post-nasal space -> nasopharyngeal cancer
Same scenario but age 4 years -> most likely adenoids
2nd most common presentation of nasopharyngeal cancer is otitis media with effusion (OME): the mass blocks the Eustachian tube
Doctor's note: any older patient with hearing loss and OME on examination -> examine the nasopharynx and take a biopsy

Clarification: many textbooks list a painless upper-neck lymph node mass as the most common single presentation of nasopharyngeal cancer; for the exam follow the doctor's emphasis (nasal obstruction, and OME in an older adult)

children.label: CT Image 7: axial, ethmoid cells and sphenoid sinus
children: Description: axial CT at level of ethmoid cells and sphenoid sinus: lamina papyracea, anterior ethmoid cells, posterior ethmoid cells, sphenoid sinus
In the axial view it is easier to differentiate anterior from posterior ethmoid cells
Always the first cell after the sphenoid is posterior, and all the cells in front of it are anterior

children.label: CT Image 8: sagittal, sinuses and post-nasal space
children: Description: sagittal CT of paranasal sinuses: frontal sinus, anterior and posterior ethmoid cells, sphenoid sinus, post-nasal space, hard palate, soft palate
The pituitary gland lies here, inside the sella turcica (just above the sphenoid sinus)
Pituitary adenoma (micro/macro adenoma) management: approach is transsphenoidal (through the nose and the sphenoid sinus)
ENT surgeon opens the way and removes the floor of the sella turcica; neurosurgeon removes the tumour

children.label: CT Image 9: sagittal, frontal sinus, sphenoid sinus, post-nasal space
children: Description: sagittal CT of paranasal sinuses showing the frontal sinus, the sphenoid sinus and the post-nasal space

children.label: MCQs - Text-based (Q11-19)
children: Q: Which artery is NOT involved in blood supply of Little's area? (A. Anterior ethmoidal; B. Greater palatine; C. Superior labial; D. Posterior ethmoidal) | A: D - Posterior ethmoidal; Little's area = anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine, superior labial arteries

Q: In an elderly patient on anticoagulants, epistaxis most commonly arises from: (A. Little's area; B. Anterior ethmoidal artery; C. Woodruff's plexus (posterior); D. Nasal vestibule) | A: C - Woodruff's plexus (posterior); typical in older patients, mainly because of anticoagulant use

Q: Recurrent anterior nosebleed does not settle on topical Fusidine and vasoconstriction. Next step after 1 week? (A. Cauterization; B. Nasal packing for 1 week; C. Septoplasty; D. Ligation of the ECA) | A: A - Cauterization; slide management: topical antibiotic, vasoconstriction, cauterization if not improved within 1 week

Q: Which sinuses open into the middle meatus? (A. Maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal; B. Posterior ethmoid and sphenoid; C. Sphenoid only; D. Maxillary and sphenoid) | A: A - Maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal, through hiatus semilunaris; posterior ethmoid -> superior meatus; sphenoid -> sphenoethmoidal recess
Q: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the: (A. Superior meatus; B. Middle meatus; C. Sphenoethmoidal recess; D. Inferior meatus) | A: D - Inferior meatus

Q: Why can infections of the nose and 'danger area' of the face spread easily to the cranial cavity? (A. Veins are valveless and communicate with cavernous sinus; B. Lymphatics drain directly into the brain; C. Nasal mucosa is keratinized; D. Septum is perforated) | A: A - veins are valveless; angular and facial veins communicate with cavernous sinus through ophthalmic veins

children.label: MCQs - Text-based (Q20-27)
children: Q: Which pair of sinuses is present at birth? (A. Frontal and sphenoid; B. Frontal and ethmoid; C. Maxillary and ethmoid; D. Sphenoid and maxillary) | A: C - Maxillary and ethmoid

Q: Thinnest part of the skull base and most common site of spontaneous CSF leak is the: (A. Cribriform plate; B. Planum sphenoidale; C. Tegmen tympani; D. Clivus) | A: A - Cribriform plate, where the middle turbinate attaches

Q: Accidental fracture of which structure during FESS can lead to CSF leak? (A. Inferior turbinate; B. Uncinate process; C. Nasal bone; D. Middle turbinate) | A: D - Middle turbinate; part of ethmoid, attaches to cribriform plate; inferior turbinate is a separate facial bone

Q: Which is NOT a complication of septoplasty? (A. Septal hematoma; B. Anosmia; C. Ophthalmoplegia ('frozen eye'); D. Septal perforation) | A: C - Ophthalmoplegia; complications: septal hematoma, perforation, nasal deformity, CSF leak, anosmia; ophthalmoplegia relates to cavernous sinus
Q: The first step in FESS is: (A. Frontal sinusotomy; B. Sphenoidotomy; C. Septoplasty; D. Uncinectomy) | A: D - Uncinectomy; uncinate process acts like a valve over maxillary sinus drainage

Q: A Haller cell is: (A. An ethmoid cell pneumatizing into the roof of the maxillary sinus; B. A frontal cell above the agger nasi; C. A sphenoid cell next to the optic nerve; D. A cyst of the nasolacrimal duct) | A: A - ethmoid cell pneumatizing into roof of maxillary sinus; a large one can narrow maxillary outflow -> risk factor for maxillary sinusitis

Q: Patient says 'Every time I have a cold, my eye swells.' Most likely anatomical reason? (A. Septal deviation; B. Lamina papyracea dehiscence; C. Cribriform plate defect; D. Haller cell) | A: B - Lamina papyracea dehiscence lets ethmoid infection spread into the orbit

Q: Which sinus is most commonly related to orbital complications, and which to cranial-nerve/optic-nerve complications? (A. Maxillary - Frontal; B. Ethmoid - Sphenoid; C. Sphenoid - Ethmoid; D. Frontal - Maxillary) | A: B - Ethmoid (orbital) - Sphenoid (cranial nerve / optic nerve)

children.label: MCQs - Text-based (Q28-35)
children: Q: The cavernous sinus contains: (A. Internal carotid artery and CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI; B. Internal jugular vein and CN IX, X, XI; C. Vertebral artery and CN XII; D. External carotid artery and CN VII) | A: A - Internal carotid artery and CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI

Q: A 'frozen eye' (ophthalmoplegia) after sphenoid sinusitis suggests: (A. Orbital cellulitis only; B. Frontal mucocele; C. Cavernous sinus thrombosis; D. Optic neuritis) | A: C - Cavernous sinus thrombosis; involvement of CN III, IV and VI causes ophthalmoplegia

children.label: Allergic rhinitis: definition and pathophysiology

Caused by IgE-mediated immunopathologic events
Sensitization: allergens contact nasal mucosa; IgE receptors are exposed over mast cells
Second exposure triggers the early- and late-phase responses
Early phase (IgE-mediated): within 5 minutes of exposure, maximum effect at 15 minutes

Released: histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4), PGD2, cytokines

Ocular: redness, itchiness, watery eyes, conjunctivitis, burning

Moderate-severe (any of the following): sleep disturbance, impairment of daily living, sport, leisure, impaired work or school, troublesome symptoms
Classification crosses intermittent / persistent with mild / moderate-severe

children.label: Allergic rhinitis: definitive testing for atopy
children: In vivo (skin testing): scratch test (not widely used)
Skin prick test: series of allergens inserted by needle into skin; positive wheal-and-flare reactions compared to controls; risk of anaphylaxis
Intradermal testing: similar to prick test except allergen placed intradermally; more sensitive than prick test; risk of anaphylaxis
In vitro: radioallergosorbent test (RAST)
RAST indications: equivocal skin-test results, high risk of anaphylaxis, skin disorders, failed immunotherapy, uncooperative patient
RAST advantages: highly specific, no risk of anaphylaxis, no effect from skin condition or medications
RAST disadvantages: less sensitive, requires up to 1-2 weeks for results, more expensive

children.label: Allergic rhinitis: treatment Level I

Prevention by avoidance: clean for dust, avoid smoke, nasal saline to cleanse mucous membranes
First-line pharmacotherapy: antihistamines, decongestants, cromolyn
Second- and third-generation antihistamines: lipid insoluble, do not cross the BBB (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine)
Topical glucocorticoids: reduce local inflammation
Cromolyn (listed at end of Level I box without further detail)

Adverse local effects: candidiasis, nasal irritation, dryness, bleeding and crusting
Adverse systemic effects: increased gastric acid production, hypertension, masks signs of infection, sodium retention
Adverse systemic effects: hypokalemia, posterior subcapsular cataracts, menstrual irregularities, aseptic necrosis of the femoral head

Criteria: symptoms not easily controlled with pharmacotherapy
Criteria: sensitive to allergens that cannot be avoided
Criteria: symptoms span two or more allergy seasons or are severe
Criteria: willing to cooperate in the immunotherapy programme
Disadvantages: reliable for multiple injections, chronic regimen (3 years), risk of worsening symptoms and anaphylactic shock
Contraindications: pregnancy, autoimmune disorders, immunocompromised patients
Contraindications: β-blockers (increase sensitivity to allergens), easily avoidable allergens, non-compliant patients

children.label: Non-allergic rhinitis: definition and infectious types
children: Group of symptoms: nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, itching and/or postnasal drainage
Not caused by IgE-mediated immunopathologic events
Infectious viral: common cold
Viral pathogens: rhinoviruses (most common), respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus

Viral symptomatic therapy: decongestants (topical and systemic), antihistamines, hydration, nasal saline irrigations, analgesics

Vasomotor theory: abnormal functioning of parasympathetic input to turbinate and septal mucosa
Vasomotor: symptoms similar to allergic rhinitis but negative allergy evaluation

Vasomotor: diagnosis of exclusion; Tx: anticholinergic sprays, corticosteroid sprays

NARES: dx allergic symptoms with negative allergic tests
NARES: symptomatic relief similar to allergic rhinitis (nasal corticosteroids, antihistamines, decongestants)
