children.label: Rhinosinusitis: definition
children: Rhinitis and sinusitis usually coexist in most individuals, so the correct term is now rhinosinusitis (RS)
Most guidelines and expert panels have adopted the term rhinosinusitis
Adults: inflammation of nose and paranasal sinuses with ≥ 2 symptoms, one of which must be nasal blockage/obstruction/congestion OR nasal discharge (anterior/posterior nasal drip)
Children: same definition, ≥ 2 symptoms, one of which must be nasal blockage OR nasal discharge
Additional symptoms in adults: facial pain/pressure; reduction or loss of smell
Additional symptoms in children: facial pain/pressure; cough
AND either endoscopic signs: nasal polyps, and/or mucopurulent discharge primarily from middle meatus, and/or oedema/mucosal obstruction primarily in middle meatus
OR CT changes: mucosal changes within the ostiomeatal complex and/or sinuses
Children: same endoscopic signs or CT changes

children.label: Rhinosinusitis: classification by duration
children: Acute: < 12 weeks with complete resolution of symptoms
Chronic: ≥ 12 weeks without complete resolution of symptoms
Alternative classification (other authors): acute 1 day – 4 weeks; subacute 4 weeks – 3 months; chronic > 3 months
Alternative chronic definition: uncontrolled or inadequately managed; process irreversible without surgical intervention
Recurrent acute: ≥ 4 episodes of acute sinusitis within 1 year with complete resolution of symptoms between attacks
Acute exacerbation of CRS: symptoms of CRS worsen but return to baseline after treatment

children.label: Acute rhinosinusitis (ARS): types
children: Viral ARS (common cold): symptoms for < 10 days
Acute post-viral RS: increase of symptoms after 5 days or persistent symptoms after 10 days, with duration < 12 weeks
Acute bacterial RS: suggested by ≥ 3 of the following
ABRS criteria: discoloured/purulent discharge (unilateral predominance); severe local pain (unilateral predominance)
ABRS criteria: fever > 38 °C; elevated ESR/CRP; 'double sickening' (deterioration after an initial milder phase)
ARS divides into common cold and post-viral RS; a small subgroup of post-viral RS is bacterial (ABRS)

children.label: ARS: CT and management
children: CT in acute sinusitis: large air-fluid level in left maxillary sinus, smaller quantity in right maxillary sinus, opacification of ethmoid cells
Left maxillary = large air-fluid level; right maxillary = small fluid; ethmoid cells = opacified → most likely diagnosis: acute sinusitis
Management of ARS slide shows endoscopic picture of mucopurulent discharge from the middle meatus (the endoscopic sign of rhinosinusitis)

children.label: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS): CRSwNP vs CRSsNP
children: CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP): bilateral polyps, endoscopically visualised in the middle meatus
CRS without nasal polyps (CRSsNP): no visible polyps in the middle meatus (if necessary after decongestant)
Prevalence: CRSwNP less prevalent; CRSsNP more prevalent
Inflammatory pattern: CRSwNP tissue eosinophilia much higher; CRSsNP neutrophil infiltration
Important to distinguish the two: clinical similarities but discrete pathologic entities with unique inflammatory and cytokine profiles that can influence treatment

children.label: CRS: pathophysiologic characteristics
children: Ostial patency: oedema (allergens, infection)
Ostial patency: polyps (atopy, CF, chronic infection)
Ostial patency: structural factors (septal deviation, Haller's cells, concha bullosa)
Ciliary function: decreased ciliary beat frequency (ciliotoxins, cold air)
Ciliary function: loss of metachronous coordination (synechiae)
Ciliary function: loss of ciliated cells (irritants/pollutants, inflammatory mediators, viral/bacterial-mediated cell death)
Mucus: changes in quantity (allergens, airway irritants/pollutants)
Mucus: changes in quality (dehydration, CF)

children.label: Nasal polyps
children: Benign semitransparent nasal lesions arising from mucosa of nasal cavity or one or more paranasal sinuses
Associated with multiple benign polyps: bronchial asthma, CF, allergic rhinitis, AFS, chronic rhinosinusitis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, aspirin intolerance, NARES
Antrochoanal polyp: single, unilateral, usually found in children
Ethmoidal polyp: bilateral, usually found in adults
Endoscopy: nasal polyp seen between the middle turbinate and nasal septum

children.label: Management of CRS
children: Medical: saline nasal irrigation – removes mucus and secretions
Medical: intranasal corticosteroids – reduce inflammation and swelling
Medical: antibiotics – when bacterial infection is suspected/indicated
Medical: treat contributing conditions (e.g. allergies)
Surgical: FESS = Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery, performed with an endoscope through the nostrils, usually without external incisions
FESS aims: widen blocked sinus drainage openings; improve drainage and ventilation
FESS aims: remove obstructing tissue when indicated; facilitate delivery of topical medications
FESS indication: symptoms persist despite appropriate medical treatment
Complications of FESS are listed on the slide heading but not detailed

children.label: Microbiology of sinusitis
children: Acute, community-acquired viral: rhinovirus (most common)
Acute, community-acquired bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common, 30%), Haemophilus influenzae (20%), Moraxella catarrhalis (20%)
Acute, community-acquired bacterial (others): other streptococci (S. pyogenes), anaerobes
Acute, nosocomial: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staph. aureus, Candida, streptococci, anaerobes
Chronic: anaerobes (Bacteroides), fungus (1–2%), alpha streptococci, H. influenzae, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis
Immunosuppression: Pseudomonas, S. aureus, Listeria monocytogenes, Legionella
Cystic fibrosis: Staph. aureus

children.label: Fungal sinusitis: types
children: Non-invasive: 1. Fungal ball (mycetoma) – fungal collection, usually in maxillary sinus, without tissue invasion
Non-invasive: 2. Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS) – allergic reaction with nasal polyps and thick allergic mucin
Invasive: 3. Acute fulminant invasive – rapidly progressive, usually immunocompromised; may invade vessels, bone, orbit, brain
Invasive: 4. Chronic invasive – progresses slowly but invades tissues
Invasive: 5. Chronic granulomatous – chronic tissue invasion with granuloma formation

children.label: Fungal ball (sinonasal mycetoma)
children: Non-invasive fungal infection forming a dense collection of fungal hyphae within a sinus cavity, most commonly the maxillary sinus
Does not invade mucosa or surrounding tissue
Chronic (months–years); usually in immunocompetent patients
Most common fungus: Aspergillus fumigatus
Coronal CT: opacified left maxillary sinus with central hyperdensity

children.label: Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS)
children: Non-invasive, chronic inflammatory condition caused by hypersensitivity reaction to fungal elements (usually Aspergillus or dematiaceous fungi), primarily in atopic individuals
Coronal CT: expanded opacified sinuses with heterogeneous hyperdense allergic mucin

children.label: AFRS: Bent and Kuhn criteria
children: All 5 major criteria must be met
1. Type I hypersensitivity: IgE-mediated allergy to fungi (positive skin prick test or serum fungal-specific IgE)
2. Nasal polyposis: nasal polyps on examination
3. Characteristic CT findings: heterogeneous sinus opacification with areas of hyperdensity (allergic mucin) and sinus expansion
4. Allergic (eosinophilic) mucin containing fungal elements: eosinophilic mucin with non-invasive fungal hyphae on histopathology
5. Absence of invasion into sinus tissue: no evidence of fungal tissue invasion (non-invasive)
Major criteria: type I hypersensitivity, nasal polyposis, characteristic CT findings, eosinophilic mucin without invasion, positive fungal stain
Minor criteria: asthma, unilateral disease, bone erosion, positive fungal culture, Charcot-Leyden crystals, serum eosinophilia
Clinical pearl: Q&A from slide – AFRS is associated with type I hypersensitivity
Clinical pearl: positive fungal stain = major criterion, while positive fungal culture = minor criterion
Clinical pearl: eosinophilic mucin without tissue invasion = major criterion

children.label: Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis (AIFR)
children: Rapidly progressive fungal infection of nasal and paranasal sinus mucosa with invasion into mucosa, blood vessels and sometimes bone
Occurs mainly in immunocompromised patients
Aggressive; may invade vessels, bone and adjacent tissues
Coronal CT: bone destruction and adjacent soft-tissue infiltration

children.label: AFRS vs fungal ball vs invasive fungal sinusitis
children: Doctor's note: students marked this table as the part the doctor focused on
Host immune status: AFRS atopic, immunocompetent; fungal ball immunocompetent; invasive immunocompromised
Fungal invasion: AFRS no; fungal ball no; invasive yes
Common organism: AFRS dematiaceous fungi, Aspergillus; fungal ball Aspergillus; invasive Mucor, Aspergillus
Symptoms: AFRS chronic, polyps, thick mucin; fungal ball chronic sinus symptoms; invasive acute, rapid, severe (fever, necrosis)
Treatment: AFRS surgery + steroids; fungal ball surgery only; invasive surgery + systemic antifungals
Recurrence: AFRS high; fungal ball low; invasive high mortality without prompt treatment

children.label: AFRS vs invasive fungal rhinosinusitis (IFRS)
children: Bone erosion: AFRS common, but due to pressure and chronic inflammation (thinning and expansion); IFRS due to fungal invasion and tissue destruction – rapid, aggressive bony destruction
Nature of erosion: AFRS smooth thinning and expansion of sinus walls; IFRS irregular, moth-eaten or punched-out destructive lesions
Speed: AFRS slow, chronic; IFRS rapid, aggressive – days to weeks
Associated findings: AFRS sinus expansion, remodelling without invasion of surrounding tissue; IFRS adjacent tissue invasion (soft tissue, orbit, brain)
Pathophysiology: AFRS non-invasive hypersensitivity reaction → mucin build-up and pressure; IFRS fungal hyphae invade mucosa, vessels, bone → necrosis
Imaging clues: AFRS expansion and thinning of bone, hyperdense allergic mucin; IFRS bone destruction with adjacent soft-tissue infiltration
Clinical implication: AFRS usually no urgent intervention; IFRS medical emergency – immediate surgery and antifungals

children.label: How to differentiate in the exam
children: 1. Invasive fungal sinusitis: usually immunocompromised patients; rapid progression over days–weeks
Invasive fungal sinusitis: aggressive bone destruction with possible extension into orbit or brain; medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and treatment
2. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC): malignant tumour of the nasopharynx (behind the nose, above the soft palate)
NPC: mass with extension into adjacent tissues or skull-base erosion
NPC: may have cervical lymph-node enlargement, nasal obstruction, or hearing loss from Eustachian tube obstruction
NPC: diagnosis must be confirmed by biopsy
Clinical pearl: if an immunocompetent patient's CT shows bone destruction and extension into adjacent tissues, other diagnoses including malignancies must also be considered
Clinical pearl: NPC cannot be diagnosed on immune status and CT alone – biopsy is required

children.label: Complications of rhinosinusitis: orbital (ophthalmological)
children: Orbital complications are the most common complication of rhinosinusitis
Ethmoid sinus is the sinus most commonly contributing to orbital complications
Third-nerve palsy may result from sphenoid sinusitis
Intra-orbital pathways: direct extension (especially through thin-walled lamina papyracea); thrombophlebitis (valveless veins)
Intra-orbital pathways: congenital dehiscence; trauma; direct lymphatics

children.label: Orbital septum
children: Fibrous membrane deep to orbicularis oculi
Extends from periosteum of the orbit to levator aponeurosis in upper eyelid and to tarsal plate in lower eyelid
Extension of periosteum into both eyelids
Separates preseptal from postseptal (orbital) disease

children.label: Chandler classification: stages I-II
children: I. Periorbital/preseptal cellulitis: prevalent in children
Stage I: orbital complications more common in children; overall incidence 3–4% of children with ARS
Stage I: spread from the ethmoid is quick and can occur even under antibiotics
Stage I: eyelid oedema, erythema, tenderness; NO vision change, chemosis, proptosis or restricted eye movements
II. Orbital cellulitis: proptosis, chemosis; may cause vision changes (afferent pupillary defect)
Stage II: children may first lose the ability to distinguish green/red colours; may limit extra-ocular muscles

children.label: Chandler classification: stages III-V
children: III. Subperiosteal abscess: pus between periorbita and lamina papyracea
Stage III: chemosis, proptosis, restricted extra-ocular motion, decreased vision; most common organism Strep. viridans
IV. Orbital abscess: pus in the orbital soft tissue; proptosis, chemosis, restricted extra-ocular motion, decreased vision
V. Cavernous sinus thrombosis: pathogens S. aureus (most common), haemolytic Streptococcus
Stage V signs: spiking fevers, toxaemia, exophthalmos, paresis of III/IV/VI, bilateral signs, reduced conscious level/cerebral irritation
Stage V treatment: IV antibiotics; may require ligation of IJV if septic emboli; anticoagulants (controversial); sinus surgery
Chemosis = swelling (oedema) of the conjunctiva, due to oozing of exudate from abnormally permeable capillaries

children.label: General management of orbital complications
children: Admission; monitor vital signs, temperature, orbit, neurological status
IV antibiotics; decongestant, nasal steroid, oral steroid; IV fluids; keep NPO; nasal douches
Investigations: CBC, inflammatory markers, blood culture, nasal swab for culture, KFT
Indications for immediate CT (with and without contrast): inability to assess vision; proptosis, chemosis; ophthalmoplegia
Indications for immediate CT: bilateral oedema; deteriorating visual acuity; no improvement after 24 h of IV antibiotics
Indications for immediate CT: swinging fevers not resolving within 36 h; signs/symptoms of CNS involvement

children.label: Neurologic and other complications
children: Neurologic: meningitis (most common intracranial complication)
Neurologic: epidural or subdural abscess; brain abscess; cavernous sinus thrombosis; venous sinus thrombosis
Consider MRI when an intracranial or intra-orbital complication is suspected
Superior orbital fissure syndrome: fixed globe, dilated pupil, ptosis (CN III, IV, VI) + hypoaesthesia of upper eyelid (CN V1)
Orbital apex syndrome = superior orbital fissure syndrome plus optic nerve involvement

children.label: Pott's puffy tumour
children: Osteomyelitis or subperiosteal abscess of the frontal bone with overlying soft-tissue swelling, by invasion of the diploic vein
Most often in adolescents and young adults; most common organism S. aureus
Infection erodes through the wall of the obstructed frontal sinus to form a subperiosteal abscess
May extend intracranially: epidural abscess, subdural empyema, meningitis, cerebral abscess
Dural sinus thrombosis is another complication
Tx: IV antibiotics, trephination, may require surgical debridement

children.label: Olfactory disorders
children: Anosmia = loss or absence of sense of smell; affects ≈ 1% of population under 60; olfactory function also decreases with ageing
Anosmia: inability to detect odours
Hyposmia: diminished olfactory sensitivity
Dysosmia: distorted identification of smell – parosmia (altered perception of smell), phantosmia (smelling nonexistent odours)
Three most common causes of anosmia: (1) sinonasal disease; (2) post-viral anosmia; (3) head trauma
Sinonasal disease: most commonly polyp disease, chronic rhinosinusitis or allergic rhinitis; the most treatable cause of anosmia
Head trauma: shearing force on olfactory filaments, olfactory bulb contusion and frontal lobe injury are proposed mechanisms

children.label: Epistaxis: causes and types
children: Children: URTIs; digital trauma (nasal picking – most common); foreign body; juvenile nasal angiofibroma
Adults: trauma; septal deviation; neoplasm; Wegener's granulomatosis; infections (bacterial/fungal)
Adults: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia)
Anterior bleed: Little's area; recurrent, self-limiting
Posterior bleed: elderly; medical comorbidities (hypertension, aspirin, warfarin); more severe
Bleeding from the nasal septum is more common than from the lateral nasal cavity; anterior is more common than posterior bleeding

children.label: Epistaxis: how to manage
children: Trotter's (Hippocratic) method: patient leans forward; local pressure over cartilaginous part of nose for at least 10–15 min; ice pack over bridge of nose
Protect the airway if needed; RESUSCITATE; rapid history; CBC, blood group, clotting profile
Then stepwise: cautery (chemical/electrical) → nasal packing (anterior/posterior) → sphenopalatine artery ligation → embolization
Nasal cautery: chemical (silver nitrate stick) or electrical
Warning: do NOT cauterize bilaterally (risk of septal perforation)

children.label: Epistaxis: nasal packing

Always cover with an anti-staphylococcal antibiotic with packing, to avoid toxic shock syndrome
Merocele packs: expandable nasal sponge packs
Posterior nasal packing: Foley / balloon catheter, 20 cc and 10 cc balloons

children.label: Overview of tonsils & adenoids
children: Doctor's note: In the original file red text = lecturer's own words; the whole Overview page and the clinical cases are the lecturer's
Role: secondary lymphoid organs responsible for secondary immunity
Primary function: act as “guards” of the Respiratory System (RS) and Digestive System (DS)
Mechanism: any antigen entering the body is recognised by M cells (antigen-presenting cells that capture the antigen)
B cells: responsible for the antigen–antibody reaction
Decision making: identify incoming pathogens and determine whether the substance is safe or harmful

children.label: Anatomy & structure of the palatine tonsils
children: Location: oropharynx, between anterior and posterior pillars
Structure: encapsulated organs containing crypts
Crypts significantly increase surface epithelial area, allowing maximum antigen exposure and recognition
Immunological memory: “memory bank of information” classifying cells/substances as “self” (safe) or “non-self” (pathogens)
Held in place by two muscles: anteriorly palatoglossal; posteriorly palatopharyngeal
Clinical pearl: Removing tonsils does not severely affect overall immunity because they are secondary immune organs
Clinical pearl: Primary immunity is supported by primary lymphoid organs (e.g. bone marrow) and systemic organs (spleen and blood)

children.label: The adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil)
children: Definition: mass of lymphoid tissue acting as a secondary immune organ to identify pathogens
Location: tight space, posterosuperiorly in nasopharynx, beneath skull base, above oropharynx, between the tubal tonsils
Restrictive location: any hypertrophy easily causes airway obstruction (airway compromise) and secondary infections

children.label: Waldeyer's ring
children: Definition: lymphoid tissue surrounding the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts
Components: paired palatine tonsils, pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), paired tubal tonsils, lingual tonsil
Palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx; adenoid lies in roof and posterior wall of nasopharynx
Sample inhaled and ingested antigens and contribute to mucosal immune responses
Physiologic enlargement is common in childhood; size alone does not determine disease severity
Doctor's note: Circular or oval arrangement of lymphoid tissues in the pharynx responsible for regional secondary immunity

children.label: Waldeyer's ring: corrected anatomical order (superior to inferior)
children: I. Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid): postero-superior, in the nasopharynx
II. Tubal tonsils: superior and bilateral (around the Eustachian tube openings)
III. Palatine tonsils: inferior and bilateral (lateral walls of the oropharynx)
IV. Lingual tonsil: antero-inferior (at the base of the tongue)

children.label: Palatine tonsil: anatomy and relations
children: Paired oval masses of lymphoid tissue in the tonsillar fossa, between palatoglossal (anterior) and palatopharyngeal (posterior) arches
Medial (mucosal) surface: non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with deep crypts
Crypts are invaginations that increase surface area for immune detection
Lateral surface: fibrous capsule; peritonsillar space separates capsule from superior constrictor muscle
Superior pole: may be related to the paratonsillar vein; inferior pole is near the tongue base
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and internal carotid artery are important deep/lateral relations; carotid anatomy varies

children.label: Palatine tonsil: arterial blood supply and venous drainage
children: Main supply: branches of the external carotid system
1. Tonsillar branch of facial artery: usually the major contributor
2. Ascending palatine branch of facial artery
3. Dorsal lingual branches of lingual artery
4. Ascending pharyngeal artery
5. Greater (descending) palatine branch of maxillary artery
Venous drainage: paratonsillar (external palatine) vein and pharyngeal venous plexus; clinically relevant to haemorrhage
Clinical pearl: All blood supply to palatine tonsils originates from the External Carotid Artery (ECA); lecturer: “all ultimately branching from the ECA”

children.label: Order of ECA branches (inferior to superior)
children: 1 Superior thyroid
2 Ascending pharyngeal
3 Lingual
4 Facial
5 Occipital
6 Posterior auricular
7 Maxillary
8 Superficial temporal
Mnemonic: Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students

children.label: Palatine tonsil: innervation, lymphatics and examination
children: Sensory innervation: glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and lesser palatine nerves from maxillary division of CN V
CN IX explains referred otalgia and contributes to postoperative throat pain
Lymph drains mainly to upper deep cervical nodes, especially the jugulodigastric node
Examination: tonsil size, symmetry, mucosal appearance, exudate, cervical lymph nodes
Unilateral enlargement, ulceration, firmness or persistent asymmetry requires appropriate assessment

children.label: Tonsillar hypertrophy grading (Brodsky)
children: Based on percentage of oropharyngeal airway obstruction
Grade 0: normal, entirely within tonsillar fossa, or surgically removed
Grade 1: < 25% of the airway
Grade 2: 26%–50% of the airway
Grade 3: 51%–75% of the airway
Grade 4: > 75% of the airway (often touching in midline = “kissing tonsils”)

children.label: Adenoid: anatomy and relations
children: Lymphoid tissue in roof and posterior wall of nasopharynx
Covered by respiratory epithelium; surface folds rather than the deep crypt pattern of palatine tonsils
Near the choanae, torus tubarius and pharyngeal openings of Eustachian tubes
Enlargement can obstruct nasal airflow and Eustachian tube function, contributing to mouth breathing and middle-ear effusion
Unlike palatine tonsils, adenoids are not normally visible on routine oral examination
Use nasoendoscopy or appropriate imaging when indicated

children.label: Adenoid: blood supply and function
children: Blood supply from branches of ascending pharyngeal, facial (including ascending palatine) and maxillary arterial systems; contributions vary
Venous drainage: pharyngeal venous plexus
Doctor's note: Adenoid blood supply primarily from the ascending pharyngeal artery; venous drainage goes toward the jugular system
Part of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT): antigen sampling and local immune responses, particularly in childhood
Commonly enlarge during childhood and often regress toward adolescence
Persistent obstruction or recurrent disease may outweigh benefit of retaining enlarged tissue
Adenoidectomy does not generally cause clinically important immune deficiency

children.label: Adenoid hypertrophy grading
children: Based on percentage of obstruction of the posterior nasal choanae
Grade 1: < 25% of the choanae
Grade 2: 26%–50% of the choanae
Grade 3: 51%–75% of the choanae
Grade 4: > 75% of the choanae (near-complete or complete nasal obstruction)

children.label: Functions of tonsils and adenoids
children: Contribute to mucosal immune surveillance and antigen presentation
Contain B and T lymphocytes; support local antibody responses, including secretory IgA
Most active during childhood, when the immune system encounters new antigens
Not essential organs; removal considered when disease burden or obstruction justifies surgery
Decision-making balances symptom severity, documented infections, comorbidities and operative risk

children.label: Acute tonsillitis: clinical approach
children: Common causes: viruses and group A Streptococcus; appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish all causes
Symptoms: sore throat, fever, odynophagia, erythematous/enlarged tonsils, exudate, tender cervical nodes
Assess hydration, airway, trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation, neck swelling, systemic toxicity
Use local guidance for rapid antigen testing/culture and antibiotics
Antibiotics are for appropriate suspected/confirmed bacterial disease
Urgent referral if airway compromise, inability to swallow fluids, suspected peritonsillar/deep neck abscess, or sepsis

children.label: Lecturer's clinical case: acute bacterial tonsillitis
children: Doctor's note: Patient: 8-year-old child with severe fatigue and 2-day history of school absence
Doctor's note: Complaints: severe sore throat, high-grade fever, inability to tolerate oral intake
Doctor's note: Exam: bilateral inflamed tonsils, tonsillar exudate, severe swelling and erythema, localized cervical lymphadenopathy
Doctor's note: Diagnosis: acute bacterial tonsillitis
Doctor's note: Most common pathogen: Group A Beta-Hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS); marked “important” in the original
Doctor's note: GABHS remains approximately 100% sensitive to penicillin; first-line Penicillin or Amoxicillin

children.label: Modified Centor criteria
children: Purpose: clinical scoring tool estimating probability that pharyngitis/tonsillitis is streptococcal
Prevents overuse of antibiotics by guiding whether to test, treat, or offer only symptomatic relief
Scoring, 1 point each: tonsillar exudate (swelling/exudate)
1 point: tender/swollen anterior cervical lymph nodes (level II)
1 point: high-grade fever > 38 °C
1 point: absence of cough
1 point: age 3–14 years
Algorithm: score 0–1 = low probability of GAS, no further testing, symptomatic treatment
Algorithm: score 2–5 = rapid strep test; if negative (school-aged children) throat culture; negative = symptomatic treatment, positive = treat
Antibiotics: PCN VK 500 mg BID × 10 d (Bicillin option)
Children/cannot swallow pills: amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/d × 10 d
PCN allergy (not anaphylaxis): cephalexin 20 mg/kg/dose BID × 10 d, or clindamycin 7 mg/kg/dose TID (300 mg/dose max) × 5 d

children.label: Clinical algorithm based on Centor score
children: Score 4–5: high probability of GABHS; proceed directly with empiric antibiotic therapy
Score 2–3: intermediate probability; Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT / rapid strep test), ≈ 95% sensitivity
Score 2–3: RADT positive → start antibiotics
Score 2–3: RADT negative but high clinical suspicion (e.g. toxic appearance) → throat culture; treat if positive, symptomatic treatment if negative
Score 0–1: highly unlikely bacterial (e.g. exudate is the only symptom); no rapid testing or throat culture, symptomatic treatment only

children.label: Infectious mononucleosis: cause and presentation
children: Usually caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), transmitted mainly through saliva
Typical features: fever, marked fatigue, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, sometimes palatal petechiae
May cause generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and atypical lymphocytosis
Diagnosis: heterophile antibody test (monospot test) in appropriate patients (star marked in the original)
EBV-specific serology may be needed early in illness or in young children
Consider streptococcal infection and other causes; a positive test for one organism does not always exclude co-infection
Infographic symptoms: fatigue, sore throat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, loss of appetite, headache
Infographic less common: rash, swollen liver or spleen, jaundice
Infographic management: no specific treatment, symptomatic
Infographic prevention: avoid close contact, good hygiene, do not share personal items

children.label: Infectious mononucleosis: management and cautions
children: Doctor's note: Since it is a viral infection, treatment is purely symptomatic
Supportive care: fluids, rest, appropriate analgesia/antipyretics
Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin when EBV suspected unless clear indication; may cause adverse reaction (prominent rash)
Systemic corticosteroids not routine; reserve for serious complications such as impending airway obstruction or selected severe haematologic complications under specialist care
Up to 40–50% of patients with EBV develop hepatosplenomegaly
Avoid contact sports and strenuous activity for at least 3 weeks from symptom onset because of splenic rupture risk
Return only when clinically well, guided by individualized assessment
Urgent assessment for breathing difficulty, inability to handle secretions, dehydration, severe abdominal pain, or suspected airway obstruction

children.label: Lecturer's clinical case: the misdiagnosed exudative tonsillitis
children: Doctor's note: Patient: severe fatigue and 5-day history of school absence
Doctor's note: Complaints: high-grade fever, severe sore throat, inability to tolerate oral intake
Doctor's note: Exam: markedly enlarged, erythematous bilateral palatine tonsils; thick, confluent white/grey exudate covering tonsillar surfaces
Doctor's note: Swelling almost reaching the midline (“kissing tonsils”)
Doctor's note: Initial misdiagnosis: mimicked acute bacterial tonsillitis (exudates); empirically given Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin/clavulanate)
Doctor's note: Turning point: few days later generalized maculopapular rash → points to viral cause: Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV)
Clinical pearl: Not all tonsillar exudates are bacterial; EBV is a classic viral cause of severe exudative tonsillitis
Clinical pearl: Rule: always avoid penicillins if EBV (infectious mononucleosis) is suspected

children.label: Further examination & diagnosis of EBV
children: Examination: cervical lymphadenopathy classically symmetric, prominently involving posterior cervical nodes
Bacterial strep typically involves the anterior nodes
CBC: absolute lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, indicating viral infection
Throat culture: to definitively rule out superimposed bacterial infection
Monospot test (heterophile antibody test): highly specific for infectious mononucleosis
Monospot used to confirm diagnosis once bacteria are ruled out (marked in the original)

children.label: Unresponsive acute tonsillitis and peritonsillar abscess
children: Scenario: acute bacterial tonsillitis failing to improve despite oral antibiotics
Failure to respond should immediately raise suspicion of Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
Quinsy is the most frequent complication of acute tonsillitis
Diagnostic rule of thumb: tonsillar asymmetry with uvula deviated to the contralateral side → treat as peritonsillar abscess until proven otherwise

children.label: Clinical presentation of peritonsillar abscess
children: Unilateral, severe swelling of peritonsillar tissues (superior pole)
Uvular deviation: abscess pushes uvula across midline to the unaffected side
Erythema and fluctuance (palpable fluid-filled sac) in the soft palate

children.label: Peritonsillar abscess: dangers and potential spread
children: Localized collection of pus that can easily spread into deeper fascial spaces if untreated
Parapharyngeal abscess: lateral spread into parapharyngeal space
Carotid space involvement: downward/lateral extension can reach the carotid sheath
Result: carotid sheath abscess or catastrophic carotid artery erosion/rupture
Clinical pearl: Primary and most definitive treatment is surgery: incision and drainage (I&D) or needle aspiration to evacuate pus
Clinical pearl: Surgical drainage must be combined with IV antibiotics to clear surrounding cellulitis and prevent systemic infection

children.label: Complications of tonsillar and adenoid hypertrophy
children: Upper-airway obstruction, habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, restless sleep, paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)
Daytime consequences: poor attention, behavioural changes, learning difficulties, morning headaches, reduced quality of life
Growth faltering, enuresis and cardiopulmonary effects can occur in significant disease
Adenoid enlargement can contribute to nasal obstruction, chronic mouth breathing, Eustachian tube dysfunction, otitis media with effusion, conductive hearing loss
Tonsil size alone does not reliably predict OSA severity; assess symptoms and risk factors

children.label: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy and facial growth
children: Clarification: Marked in the original as “not read” (not covered by the lecturer)
Chronic nasal obstruction may encourage habitual mouth breathing and altered head/mandibular posture
Reported associations: long/narrow facial pattern, increased lower facial height, high-arched palate, dental crowding, anterior open bite, malocclusion
Often described as “adenoid facies” pattern, but facial appearance is not diagnostic and not caused by adenoids alone
Genetics, nasal disease, oral habits and baseline craniofacial anatomy also contribute
Persistent obstruction with dental/orofacial effects warrants ENT assessment and, when appropriate, dental/orthodontic evaluation
Surgery does not guarantee reversal of established changes

children.label: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy: clinical presentation
children: Scenario: child with severely enlarged tonsils, no signs of acute infection (no exudate or acute erythema)
Bilateral massive tonsillar enlargement almost completely obstructing oropharyngeal airway
Key symptoms: loud snoring and choking episodes during sleep (OSA)
Decreased oral intake (dysphagia) from mechanical obstruction
Obligate mouth breathing; airway compromise and systemic impact
General appearance: chronically fatigued and exhausted due to fragmented sleep and intermittent hypoxia
Behavioural changes: abnormal behaviour, hyperactivity, poor concentration, declining academic performance
Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the most common cause of upper airway obstruction and compromise in paediatric population
Clinical pearl: Always suspect upper airway obstruction in a chronically fatigued child with unexplained behavioural issues

children.label: Complications of adenotonsillar hypertrophy (table)
children: Craniofacial changes (“adenoid facies”): chronic mouth breathing → structural facial alterations
Adenoid facies: 1. Retrognathia (recessed lower jaw, from keeping mouth open constantly)
Adenoid facies: 2. Prominent upper teeth (dental malocclusion and overjet)
Adenoid facies: 3. High-arched hard palate
Allergic manifestations (often coexisting): allergic shiners = dark circles/“black spots” under eyes from venous congestion
Dennie-Morgan lines: accentuated folds/creases just below lower eyelids; strongly indicate severe underlying allergies or atopy
Otologic (Eustachian tube dysfunction): hypertrophied adenoid obstructs Eustachian tube opening → negative middle-ear pressure → fluid accumulation = otitis media with effusion (OME)
OME increases susceptibility to recurrent acute otitis media
Untreated: chronic fluid → conductive hearing loss, which can significantly delay speech and language development
Mechanism: enlarged adenoids → Eustachian tube obstruction → negative middle-ear pressure → fluid accumulation → OME → increased risk of recurrent AOM

children.label: Indications for adenoidectomy
children: 1. Persistent nasal obstruction or sleep-disordered breathing attributable to adenoid hypertrophy
Airway obstruction is the most common indication for adenoidectomy
2. Documented OSA or significant obstruction, often as part of adenotonsillectomy when tonsils also contribute
3. Otitis media with effusion or recurrent middle-ear disease in selected children (age, history, guideline criteria); may be combined with tympanostomy tubes
4. Chronic/recurrent adenoiditis or paediatric chronic rhinosinusitis despite appropriate medical treatment
5. Hyponasal speech or other functional problems attributable to adenoid enlargement after appropriate assessment
Clinical pearl: Before adenoidectomy assess risk of velopharyngeal insufficiency: cleft palate, submucous cleft, bifid uvula, or pre-existing palatal dysfunction

children.label: Indications for tonsillectomy: 1. Recurrent infection (tonsillitis)
children: Watchful waiting if fewer than 7 episodes in 1 year, fewer than 5/year for 2 years, or fewer than 3/year for 3 years
Tonsillectomy may be offered when ≥ 7 episodes in past year, ≥ 5/year for 2 years, or ≥ 3/year for 3 years (the 7-5-3 rule)
Each episode documented, with sore throat plus at least one: temperature > 38.3 °C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive group A Streptococcus test
Modifying factors even if thresholds not met: multiple antibiotic allergies/intolerance
Modifying factors: PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous Stomatitis, Pharyngitis and Adenitis syndrome)
Modifying factors: more than one peritonsillar abscess
Guideline thresholds support shared decision-making; not an automatic mandate for surgery

children.label: Paradise criteria for recurrent tonsillitis
children: Frequency (must meet one): 7 episodes in past 1 year
Or 5 episodes per year in past 2 consecutive years
Or 3 episodes per year in past 3 consecutive years
Plus at least one per episode: (1) high-grade fever, (2) cervical lymphadenopathy (tender or enlarged nodes), (3) tonsillar exudate, (4) positive rapid strep test or culture for GABHS
Figure legend: fever ≥ 38.3 °C, cervical lymphadenopathy > 2 cm; documented in medical records; adequate antibiotic treatment

children.label: Indications for tonsillectomy: 2-7. Other indications
children: 2. Airway obstruction: tonsillectomy recommended for children with OSA documented by overnight polysomnography
Adenotonsillectomy is common when both tonsils and adenoids obstruct
3. Suspicion of malignancy: unilateral tonsillar enlargement with suspicious features requires evaluation for neoplasia rather than routine observation
4. Febrile seizures when triggered by recurrent tonsillitis
5. Other selected indications: recurrent peritonsillar abscess, severe dysphagia attributable to tonsils, or cardiopulmonary complications
6. Consider associated growth problems, poor school performance, enuresis, asthma, or behavioural problems in sleep-disordered breathing
7. Tonsilloliths (tonsil stones) causing severe and persistent halitosis (relative indication)
Clarification: Consider PSG in high-risk children and when symptom severity and examination are discordant; counsel that OSA can persist or recur

children.label: Complications of adenotonsillectomy
children: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage: primary (within 24 hours) or secondary (after 24 hours); potentially life-threatening
Pain, poor oral intake, dehydration, nausea/vomiting, delayed return to normal diet
Respiratory complications: laryngospasm, airway obstruction, desaturation or worsening OSA
Respiratory risk higher in young children and severe OSA
Less common: infection, dental/lip/tongue injury, taste disturbance, velopharyngeal insufficiency/hypernasal speech, nasopharyngeal stenosis, anaesthetic complications
Adenoidectomy-specific risks: injury near Eustachian tube openings and persistent/residual adenoid tissue
Clinical pearl: Any fresh bleeding after tonsillectomy is an emergency: urgent hospital assessment; do not reassure or manage at home

children.label: Adenotonsillectomy: preoperative planning
children: Confirm indication; document infection history or sleep symptoms
Review comorbidities, medications, allergies, bleeding history, prior anaesthesia issues
Assess airway, hydration, weight/BMI, craniofacial features, signs of active infection
Consider PSG and specialist/anaesthesia planning for high-risk children
Discuss expected benefit, pain, bleeding, dehydration, respiratory risk, possible persistent OSA, alternative options
Use evidence-based analgesia; single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose recommended for children undergoing tonsillectomy (AAO-HNS guideline)
Routine perioperative antibiotics not recommended for uncomplicated paediatric tonsillectomy

children.label: Postoperative monitoring and discharge advice
children: Consider overnight inpatient monitoring after tonsillectomy if child is under 3 years or has severe OSA (per AAO-HNS guidance)
Severe OSA: AHI ≥ 10 obstructive events/hour, oxygen saturation nadir < 80%, or both
Clear analgesia instructions using appropriate acetaminophen and/or ibuprofen protocols
Avoid codeine in children under 12 years after tonsillectomy
Encourage regular fluids; explain expected throat pain and referred ear pain
Urgent assessment for blood in saliva/vomit, breathing difficulty, inability to drink, markedly reduced urination, or uncontrolled pain
Follow up persistent snoring/apnoeas, ongoing nasal obstruction, voice changes, or recurrent symptoms

children.label: Roadmap & learning objectives
children: Roadmap: core anatomy → benign & malignant lesions → paediatric airway emergencies → emergency airway procedures
Describe the laryngeal framework and the anatomy of the vocal folds
Differentiate common benign vocal-fold lesions from red flags for malignancy

children.label: Laryngeal anatomy – overview
children: Cardinal functions of the larynx: airway protection, voice production (phonation), swallowing
The larynx extends from C3 to C6
Structures: cartilages · membranes · ligaments · muscles · mucous membrane

children.label: Laryngeal cartilages, membranes & landmarks
children: Unpaired cartilages: thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, epiglottis
Paired cartilages: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform
Key landmarks: hyoid → thyrohyoid membrane → thyroid → cricothyroid membrane → cricoid → trachea
The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway
Know the cricothyroid membrane clinically: it is the emergency front-of-neck airway landmark
Doctor's note: laryngeal membranes – the external membranes differ from the internal membranes and act as barriers to tumour spread
Doctor's note: function of membranes and ligaments – anatomical barriers resisting tumour spread between the different regions of the larynx, but they do not completely prevent the spread

children.label: Laryngeal muscles
children: Extrinsic muscles: elevate and depress the larynx during swallowing
Intrinsic muscles: control breathing and voice production by moving the vocal cords

children.label: Laryngeal compartments
children: Supraglottis: epiglottis · aryepiglottic folds (mucosal folds connecting the epiglottis to the arytenoid cartilage) · false vocal folds · arytenoid
Glottis: true vocal folds · anterior commissure · posterior commissure
Subglottis: from below the true vocal folds to the inferior border of the cricoid
Clinical pearl: lesions of the glottis commonly present early with hoarseness
Clinical pearl: airway compromise can arise from any compartment when obstruction becomes significant

children.label: Vocal fold anatomy – high yield
children: True vocal fold: stratified squamous epithelium · lamina propria · vocalis muscle
Reinke's space: a space in the superficial layer of the lamina propria of the true vocal fold that can expand
Anterior commissure: true vocal folds meet anteriorly; important landmark in laryngeal tumours
Posterior glottis: arytenoids + posterior commissure; important for airway and abduction
The membranous vocal fold is the main vibrating portion
The posterior glottis contains the arytenoid cartilages and is critical for airway opening
True vocal cord function: phonation (voice production)
Layers of the vocal folds (cover–transition–body model): mucosa/cover (epithelium, superficial lamina propria); vocal ligament (intermediate and deep lamina propria); body (vocalis muscle)

children.label: Vocal fold function and innervation
children: Abduction: posterior cricoarytenoid – the only abductor of the vocal folds
Adduction: lateral cricoarytenoid + interarytenoid + thyroarytenoid
Motor nerve: recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve → cricothyroid
Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve → sensation above the vocal folds
Recurrent laryngeal nerve → sensation below the vocal folds + motor supply to most intrinsic muscles

children.label: Direct vs indirect laryngoscopy
children: Direct laryngoscopy: true vocal cords viewed away from you, as in a patient under anaesthesia in the operating room
Indirect laryngoscopy: true vocal cords viewed toward you, as in a patient examined in the clinic
Clinic view: left and right are reversed because the patient faces you
Operating-room view: sides match your own orientation because you are positioned at the patient's head
Doctor's note (translated from Arabic): office (clinic) view – reverse the directions (image's right side is the patient's left, and vice versa); operating-room view – same directions, no reversal

children.label: Paediatric larynx
children: Clinical pearl: paediatric larynx is high and anterior compared with adults
Clinical pearl: infants are obligate nasal breathers in the first months, so nasal obstruction may cause respiratory distress
Clinical pearl: high position of larynx and epiglottis means the epiglottis may be visible on oral examination in young children

children.label: Symptoms of laryngeal pathology
children: Doctor's note: laryngeal pathology may present with hoarseness of voice, stridor, or swallowing dysfunction (dysphagia)
Doctor's note: there is a difference between acute and chronic hoarseness, and between acute and chronic stridor (translated from Arabic)
Example: 20-year-old with URTI, then voice change for 3 days → acute viral laryngitis (most likely) – supportive management
Example: asthmatic patient, immunocompromised by oral steroids, voice change for ~3 weeks → fungal laryngitis
Example: 60-year-old heavy smoker with weight loss → suspect laryngeal cancer (laryngeal malignancy)

children.label: Acute vs chronic stridor
children: Acute stridor – think of two main causes: infection and allergy
Infection: viral → supportive treatment; bacterial → antibiotics

Allergy: may cause angioedema – swelling of the laryngeal region obstructing the airway (e.g. severe allergic reaction after a particular food → laryngeal swelling affecting airflow through the vocal cords)
Severe cases need urgent airway management and may need emergency tracheostomy if the airway cannot be secured otherwise; may be life-threatening
Chronic stridor – chronic causes narrowing the airway: tumour (laryngeal tumour) causing airway compression · supraglottic mass · laryngeal web · benign laryngeal lesion

children.label: Benign vocal cord lesions – overview
children: Nodules: usually bilateral and symmetric; associated with voice misuse/phonotrauma; classically at junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3
Polyp: usually unilateral; may follow phonotrauma; pedunculated or sessile; hoarseness is common
Reinke's oedema: diffuse oedema of the superficial lamina propria; strong association with smoking; deep/low voice
Clinical pearl: benign lesions often cause dysphonia without progressive constitutional symptoms, but persistent hoarseness still needs laryngeal examination

children.label: Vocal cord nodules vs polyps
children: Affected groups – nodules: female patients · teachers · singers · paediatric age group, especially children who shout frequently · mothers who frequently shout or strain their voices
Affected groups – polyps: adult males
Causes – nodules: voice misuse / phonotrauma
Causes – polyps: voice abuse · vocal cord trauma following surgery · GERD
Management of nodules: 1. voice rest
Nodules: 2. treat contributing factors – nasal steroids (nasal inflammation/congestion); PPIs for GERD
Nodules: 3. speech therapy if symptoms persist
Nodules: 4. refractory → direct laryngoscopy with surgical excision
Management of polyps: direct laryngoscopy with surgical excision

children.label: Reinke's oedema
children: Case: 60–70-year-old female with a 50-year history of heavy smoking and a deep, husky, masculine voice → Reinke's oedema
Reinke's oedema = diffuse laryngeal oedema, ‘smoker's oedema’
Treatment: stop smoking; surgery – marsupialization

children.label: Vocal process (contact) granuloma
children: Anterior vocal fold lesion: toward the anterior commissure, where the two vocal folds meet at the front of the larynx
Posterior vocal fold lesion: toward the posterior commissure, near the arytenoid cartilages and vocal processes at the back of the larynx
Presentation: usually unilateral; bilateral cases very rare
Causes: trauma such as endotracheal intubation injuring the vocal process · GERD
Treatment: correct the underlying cause · steroid therapy · surgery in refractory cases

children.label: Other benign / premalignant lesions & red flag
children: Contact granuloma: often a posterior glottic lesion; irritation, reflux and intubation
Vocal fold cyst: subepithelial lesion causing persistent dysphonia
Papilloma/RRP: HPV-related; hoarseness and airway obstruction
Leukoplakia: white plaque; not a diagnosis by itself, biopsy may be required because dysplasia/carcinoma can be present
Red flag: persistent unilateral lesion, ulceration, fixation or progressive hoarseness → evaluate for malignancy

children.label: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP)
children: Appearance: exophytic, cauliflower-like or grape-like lesions
Causative agent: HPV types 6 and 11; HPV 11 may be associated with more aggressive disease
Commonly discussed in the paediatric age group
HPV is sexually transmitted, but transmission to children occurs by vertical (perinatal) transmission during vaginal delivery
Behaviour: may have an aggressive course (particularly HPV 11); very high recurrence rate even after treatment
Treatment: surgical debulking · CO2 laser ablation
Vaccination: Gardasil (quadrivalent) protects against HPV 6, 11, 16 and 18
Tracheostomy is generally avoided in RRP because it may promote distal spread of papillomatosis into the tracheobronchial tree

children.label: Vocal cord leukoplakia
children: Case: 60-year-old heavy smoker with hoarseness for 1 year; direct laryngoscopy shows a white, non-scrapable lesion on the vocal cord → vocal cord leukoplakia (borderline lesion)
Management: biopsy to assess the degree of dysplasia (mild, moderate or severe)
Dysplasia does not breach the basement membrane; if breached → invasive carcinoma
Treatment follows the biopsy result and degree of dysplasia

children.label: Fungal infection of the vocal cord
children: Doctor's note: risk factors – chemotherapy, immunocompromised patients, corticosteroids, prolonged antibiotic courses, asthmatic patients using inhaled corticosteroids
Doctor's note: acute presentation, usually 1–3 weeks
Doctor's note: may resemble leukoplakia, but the clinical history and duration help differentiate

children.label: Malignant vocal cord lesions
children: Most important diagnosis: laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is the key malignancy to recognize
Glottic tumours often present with hoarseness relatively early
Smoking and alcohol are major risk factors; HPV is relevant to some head and neck sites
Diagnosis requires direct visualization and tissue diagnosis
Red flags: persistent hoarseness · haemoptysis · odynophagia/dysphagia · neck mass · stridor or airway symptoms · weight loss/otalgia

children.label: Suspected laryngeal cancer – what to ask / examine
children: Duration and progression of hoarseness
Smoking/tobacco and alcohol exposure
Dysphagia or odynophagia
Stridor, dyspnoea or haemoptysis
Neck swelling and referred otalgia
Previous laryngeal lesions, surgery, intubation or irradiation
Flexible nasolaryngoscopy: inspect both vocal folds, mobility, lesion extent and airway
Case: old-age patient, heavy smoker, history of radiation exposure, family history of head and neck cancer, with a vocal cord lesion → cancer until proven otherwise
Management: direct laryngoscopy with biopsy for histopathological confirmation

children.label: Paediatric airway emergencies – airway foreign bodies
children: Typical presentation: sudden choking/coughing · stridor or wheeze · voice change · respiratory distress
Common sites: larynx · trachea · main bronchi (right main bronchus is a common bronchial site)
Key principle: suspect aspiration after a witnessed choking episode even if the child temporarily improves
Exam pearl: complete obstruction = immediate life-threatening emergency
Exam pearl: do not delay definitive airway management for unnecessary imaging when the clinical picture is obvious

children.label: Foreign body – first response and removal
children: Assess responsiveness and effective cough
Severe obstruction: activate emergency response; age-appropriate choking manoeuvres
If unresponsive: begin CPR and follow the resuscitation algorithm
Once stabilized: urgent ENT/anaesthesia assessment
Rigid bronchoscopy is commonly used for removal of significant airway foreign bodies
Note: coins swallowed by children usually pass into the oesophagus (ingestion) and may pass into the stomach
Note: seeds and nuts are more likely to enter the tracheobronchial tree (aspiration)

children.label: Foreign body – case, danger signs and management
children: Case: child with recurrent choking and witnessed aspiration while eating nuts, followed by coughing
Danger signs: stridor or a valve-like breathing sound · drooling · tripod position (sitting and leaning forward) · respiratory distress
Management: ABC assessment · do not agitate the patient (especially with respiratory distress)
Call an experienced airway team (do not work alone) and prepare for emergency airway management
Do not force the child to open the mouth or perform unnecessary oral examination if critical upper airway obstruction is suspected
Clinical pearl: any child with foreign body aspiration, even if comfortable afterwards, is at risk of sudden complete obstruction and collapse

Clinical pearl: after choking and coughing followed by temporary relief, the foreign body may have passed into the tracheobronchial tree; child may appear stable but later develop post-obstructive pneumonia (after ~2–3 days, variable)
Clinical pearl: such a child should not be sent home without proper assessment – consult paediatrics, chest X-ray, and consider bronchoscopy
Clinical pearl: a foreign body may remain even if the child is comfortable and the chest X-ray is normal

children.label: Croup
children: Typical features: viral upper-airway illness · barking cough · hoarseness · inspiratory stridor · usually worse at night
Severity – mild: stridor only with agitation
Severity – moderate/severe: stridor at rest + increased work of breathing
Severity – impending failure: fatigue, altered consciousness, hypoxia
Treatment: corticosteroid for significant symptoms · nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe croup · oxygen if hypoxaemic
Escalate airway support if deterioration; endotracheal intubation rarely required (impending respiratory failure)
Keep the child calm and avoid unnecessary distress
Age: usually 6 months to 2 years; presentation: usually mild
Cause: parainfluenza virus types 1, 2, 3 and 4; type 1 is the most common

children.label: Epiglottitis / supraglottitis
children: Red flags: high fever · toxic appearance · drooling · dysphagia/odynophagia · muffled voice · tripod position
Critical rule: do NOT force oral examination or agitate a child with suspected epiglottitis
Management: airway first in a controlled setting · experienced anaesthesia/ENT team · IV antibiotics after the airway is secured
Compared with croup: drooling + toxic appearance + muffled voice strongly increase concern for supraglottitis
Cause: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib); after the Hib vaccine, incidence of Hib epiglottitis decreased significantly
X-ray sign: thumb sign (epiglottitis)
Exam pearl: do not rely on a radiograph when a child is clinically unstable – secure the airway

children.label: Croup vs epiglottitis
children: Croup: barking cough · hoarseness · gradual onset · viral · usually nontoxic · steeple sign may be seen
Epiglottitis: drooling · muffled voice · severe odynophagia · rapid progression · toxic appearance · airway emergency
Thumb sign (epiglottitis) vs steeple sign (croup)

children.label: Airway surgery – tracheostomy types and indications
children: Types: open surgical tracheostomy · percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy
Timing/setting: elective vs emergency · temporary vs long-term
Indications: upper-airway obstruction · prolonged ventilation · airway protection · secretion management · facilitate major head & neck surgery
Exact technique and level depend on anatomy, urgency, age and operator expertise

children.label: Tracheostomy indications – doctor's explanations
children: Doctor's note – prolonged ventilation: a ventilated patient cannot keep the endotracheal tube for a long time, since it may cause subglottic stenosis and inflammation between tube and mucosa, leading to airway narrowing
Doctor's note – upper airway obstruction: such as tumour, trauma, or RTA (road traffic accident)
Doctor's note – bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): a patient with alveolar infection may need lavage; normal saline is introduced and irrigated through the tracheostomy, depending on the case

children.label: Percutaneous tracheostomy
children: Used for high-risk patients with contraindications to surgery due to anaesthesia risks or comorbidities, or who are bedridden
Performed at the bedside instead of transferring the patient to the operating room

children.label: Tracheostomy tubes
children: Cuffed: provides a seal for positive-pressure ventilation; may reduce gross aspiration of secretions
Uncuffed: used when a cuff is not required; allows airflow around the tube when the upper airway is patent
Fenestrated: has an opening that permits airflow toward the upper airway in selected patients; needs appropriate assessment
Tube selection depends on indication, age, anatomy, ventilation requirements and secretion burden
Cuffed tube: used in patients at risk of aspiration (stroke, severe dysphagia); cuff reduces but does not completely prevent aspiration/microaspiration
Cuffed tube may also be used in patients requiring positive-pressure ventilation
Tube types shown: cuffed with disposable inner cannula; cuffed with reusable inner cannula; uncuffed/disposable (for tracheal problems or patients ready for decannulation)
Tube parts: obturator, connector, flange, inflation line, pilot cuff, tube ties, side-port connector

children.label: Tracheostomy – surgical anatomy
children: Identify the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage and tracheal rings
Stay in the midline and avoid lateral vascular structures
Commonly through the upper tracheal rings, per anatomy and surgical plan
Know the thyroid isthmus and its relation to the trachea
Maintain a controlled airway throughout

children.label: Tracheostomy – key operative steps
children: 1. Position and prepare the patient; establish a secure airway/ventilation plan
2. Identify landmarks and make the skin incision
3. Dissect through subcutaneous tissue and strap muscles in the midline
4. Manage the thyroid isthmus when required
5. Expose the trachea and confirm the intended tracheal level
6. Create the tracheal opening using the chosen technique
7. Insert the tube, inflate the cuff if present, confirm ventilation and secure the tube
8. Document tube type/size and provide postoperative airway care

children.label: Tracheostomy – positioning, incision and timing
children: Positioning: neck hyperextended to bring the trachea anteriorly
Incision: midway between the cricoid cartilage and the suprasternal notch
Tracheal opening: between the 2nd and 3rd rings in ~80%; alternatively between the 3rd and 4th rings
Too low: risk of complications from nearby major vessels and the clavicular region
Too high (close to the cricoid): may cause fibrosis and subglottic stenosis
Time: emergency tracheostomy – airway secured immediately, potentially within 2 minutes; elective (operating room) ≈ 30–40 minutes

children.label: Tracheostomy – layers and dissection
children: 1. Skin – first layer incised
2. Superficial cervical fascia – contains the platysma
3. Fat and subcutaneous tissue – dissected to expose deeper layers
4. Middle cervical fascia – covers the infrahyoid muscles; dissect in the midline to separate them
5. Deep cervical fascia – dissection continues through deeper layers to expose the trachea
6. Pretracheal fascia – overlies the trachea
7. Trachea – identify the rings and select the site for opening

Note: the platysma is associated with the superficial cervical fascia; the infrahyoid muscles are covered by the middle layer of the deep cervical fascia; midline dissection provides access to the trachea

children.label: Tracheostomy – complications
children: Early complications: bleeding · false passage · pneumothorax · tube obstruction/dislodgement · subcutaneous emphysema
Late complications: stomal infection · granulation tissue · tracheal stenosis · tracheo-oesophageal fistula · tracheo-innominate fistula
Emergency: sudden respiratory distress after tracheostomy → assess tube patency, displacement and obstruction immediately
Clinical pearl: tracheo-innominate artery fistula (TIF) – abnormal communication between the trachea and the innominate (brachiocephalic) artery; can cause massive, life-threatening bleeding

children.label: Cricothyrotomy (cricothyroidotomy)
children: When: cannot intubate + cannot oxygenate/ventilate using conventional methods
Landmark: cricothyroid membrane – between the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage
Purpose: rapid emergency access to the airway – a bridge to definitive airway management
Step 1: identify thyroid cartilage → cricothyroid membrane → cricoid cartilage
Step 2: maintain oxygenation as much as possible while preparing the emergency airway
Step 3: open the cricothyroid membrane using the appropriate device/technique
Step 4: insert the airway tube/device and confirm ventilation
Step 5: secure the device and transition to definitive airway management when appropriate
Important: technique varies by equipment and age; follow local emergency protocols; emergency procedure for trained clinicians
Important: in children, age-specific airway techniques are required because of anatomy and stenosis risk

children.label: Cricothyrotomy vs tracheostomy
children: Setting: cricothyrotomy – emergency; tracheostomy – usually controlled surgical airway
Access: cricothyrotomy – fast access through the cricothyroid membrane; tracheostomy – through the anterior trachea
Duration: cricothyrotomy – usually temporary / bridge; tracheostomy – can be long-term
Exam pearl: know the anatomical landmark and the clinical indication for each

children.label: Clinical integration – approach to hoarseness
children: Acute hoarseness: infection, voice misuse, acute inflammation
Persistent hoarseness: benign lesion, malignancy, vocal-fold paralysis or other pathology
Ask about duration, smoking, reflux symptoms, voice use, dysphagia, weight loss and airway symptoms
Persistent or concerning symptoms → laryngeal visualization
Unilateral vocal-fold lesion + persistent hoarseness = do not assume benign disease

children.label: Case 1 – persistent hoarseness
children: Case: 58-year-old man with 3 months of progressive hoarseness, long-term smoker, no fever; flexible laryngoscopy shows irregular unilateral lesion involving one true vocal fold
Questions: 1. Main differentials? 2. Red flags? 3. Next diagnostic step? 4. Which examination findings must be documented?
Clarification: most important concern – laryngeal SCC
Clarification: red flags – age, smoking, progressive persistent hoarseness, irregular unilateral lesion
Clarification: assess vocal-fold mobility, lesion location/extent and cervical lymph nodes
Clarification: direct laryngoscopy with biopsy when tissue diagnosis is indicated
Clarification: staging and treatment depend on site, extent, nodal/distant disease and multidisciplinary assessment
Teaching point: persistent unilateral vocal-fold lesions require assessment for malignancy and tissue diagnosis

children.label: Case 2 – paediatric airway emergency
children: Case: 3-year-old develops sudden choking while eating, coughs violently, then develops persistent stridor and respiratory distress
Questions: 1. Most likely diagnosis? 2. Immediate priority? 3. What to avoid? 4. When is bronchoscopy considered?
Clarification: most likely diagnosis – aspirated airway foreign body
Clarification: immediate priority – assess severity and maintain oxygenation/ventilation; if severe obstruction, age-appropriate emergency choking management
Clarification: once stabilized – urgent ENT/anaesthesia assessment; rigid bronchoscopy for definitive removal
Clarification: avoid agitating the child or forcing an oral examination
Teaching point: sudden choking followed by stridor strongly suggests an airway foreign body

children.label: High-yield take-home points
children: Exam pearl: know the vocal folds, anterior/posterior commissures, cricoid and cricothyroid membrane
Persistent hoarseness + suspicious unilateral lesion → exclude malignancy
Croup, epiglottitis and foreign bodies can deteriorate rapidly
Emergency airway procedures require trained clinicians, appropriate equipment and local protocols
