children.label: Course of CN VII: brainstem to geniculate ganglion
children: Brainstem: arises from four nuclei; intrapontine fascicles exit at the cerebellopontine angle
Facial motor nucleus lies in the caudal pons
Internal acoustic meatus (meatal segment): travels with CN VIII, then enters the facial canal in the temporal bone
In the temporal bone it runs near the vestibular and cochlear regions
Labyrinthine segment: first segment inside temporal bone; shortest and narrowest; ends at geniculate ganglion
Geniculate ganglion: sensory ganglion
Geniculate ganglion gives greater petrosal nerve (1st branch): parasympathetic fibres for lacrimation and nasal and palatal gland secretion

children.label: Course of CN VII: tympanic segment to parotid
children: Tympanic (horizontal) segment: runs posteriorly along medial middle-ear wall, above the oval window; particularly vulnerable to injury
Mastoid (vertical) segment: descends to the stylomastoid foramen
Mastoid segment branches: nerve to stapedius (supplies stapedius muscle in middle ear)
Mastoid segment branches: chorda tympani = taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue + parasympathetic (secretomotor) fibres to submandibular and sublingual glands; joins the lingual nerve
Stylomastoid foramen: nerve exits the skull, gives extracranial branches, then enters parotid gland
Extracranial branches: posterior auricular nerve, branch to posterior belly of digastric, branch to stylohyoid
Parotid gland: upper temporofacial and lower cervicofacial divisions → plexus → five terminal branches supplying muscles of facial expression
Five terminal branches: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical

children.label: Course notes and clarifications
children: Note: terminal branches are motor; facial nerve traverses the parotid but does not provide the gland's secretomotor innervation
Note: facial nerve runs between the superficial and deep lobes of the parotid gland
Important distinction: marginal mandibular branch of CN VII is different from the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
Clarification: the four nuclei (Fig. 3) = motor nucleus of facial (SVE); lacrimatory and superior salivatory nuclei (GVE); nucleus of tractus solitarius (SVA); spinal nucleus of trigeminal (GSA)

children.label: Terminal branches and muscles supplied
children: Temporal: frontalis, orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii
Zygomatic: orbicularis oculi (lower part)
Buccal: orbicularis oris, buccinator, zygomaticus + muscles of the nose (e.g. nasalis)
Marginal mandibular: mentalis, depressor labii inferioris, depressor anguli oris
Cervical: platysma

children.label: CN VII functional components
children: Branchial motor (SVE): facial expression muscles, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric
Parasympathetic (GVE): lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual, nasal and palatal glands
Special sensory (SVA): taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani
General sensory (GSA): small area of the external ear / external auditory canal

children.label: Nuclear anatomy and brainstem
children: Clinical pearl: facial weakness is only one part of the facial nerve examination; do not examine facial expression alone, as the nerve has several other functions
Facial motor nucleus lies in the caudal pons
Motor fibres loop around the abducens (VI) nucleus, forming the internal genu and facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle
Nervus intermedius carries taste, sensory and parasympathetic fibres alongside the motor root
Corticobulbar input: upper facial muscles receive bilateral cortical input; lower facial muscles receive predominantly contralateral input
Central lesion: contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing (forehead has bilateral cortical supply)
Brainstem lesions may affect the whole ipsilateral face

children.label: Facial nerve functions and examination
children: Motor: raise eyebrows, wrinkle forehead, close eyes tightly, smile/show teeth, puff cheeks, purse lips
Taste: anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani
Lacrimation: greater petrosal pathway; assess dry eye and tearing history
Stapedius: hyperacusis may occur with proximal lesions
Salivation: submandibular/sublingual glands via chorda tympani
Inspect: ear canal, pinna, oral cavity, parotid, and complete cranial nerves
Doctor's note: raise the eyebrows → assesses frontalis
Doctor's note: close the eyes tightly → orbicularis oculi
Doctor's note: puff out the cheeks → buccinator
Doctor's note: smile and show the teeth → muscles of facial expression, particularly around the mouth
Doctor's note: these movements assess the major motor functions of CN VII and help evaluate muscles supplied by its different branches

children.label: Localizing the lesion (clinical clues)
children: Brainstem: other cranial nerve signs, gaze abnormalities, ataxia, or long-tract findings
Proximal to / near geniculate ganglion: facial weakness may accompany reduced tearing, taste disturbance and hyperacusis
Between greater petrosal & stapedius branches: tearing may be preserved, but hyperacusis/taste symptoms may occur
Distal to chorda tympani: mainly motor weakness; taste and lacrimation may be preserved
Extracranial / parotid: facial weakness with a parotid mass, pain, or progressive course is a concern

children.label: Facial nerve disorders (differential diagnosis)
children: Idiopathic: Bell's palsy (acute peripheral facial palsy after exclusion of other causes)
Viral / infectious: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV), Lyme disease (epidemiologically relevant), HIV, otitis media, mastoiditis
Traumatic / iatrogenic: temporal bone fracture, penetrating injury, parotid, ear and skull-base surgery
Neoplastic: parotid malignancy, facial nerve schwannoma, temporal bone or skull-base tumour, perineural spread
Neurologic / systemic: stroke (central pattern), brainstem disease, Guillain–Barré, sarcoidosis, diabetes
Note: congenital or recurrent/bilateral palsy requires a broader work-up
Left facial palsy signs: left forehead flattening; mouth deviated to the right (toward healthy side); incomplete left eye closure

children.label: Clinical assessment and when to investigate
children: Initial assessment of suspected facial nerve palsy = history taking + physical examination; sometimes these alone are sufficient
Example 1, first episode of Bell's palsy: previously healthy, acute palsy, dramatic improvement with treatment → typical Bell's; further investigations may not be necessary
Example 2, recurrent palsy: right-sided, second episode same side 2 months later, then a third → needs further investigation; same side repeatedly affected, consider underlying cause such as tumour
Example 3, 4-year-old with facial asymmetry during crying: take history of trauma and infection; examine ear for otitis media; if ear normal, further investigations may be needed
Example 4, palsy with neck mass: facial nerve palsy and neck swelling = major red flag for possible parotid malignancy
Example 5, palsy after road traffic accident: 5 days later difficulty closing eye and mouth deviation → consider trauma; temporal bone fracture may be responsible
Key clinical point: not every facial palsy needs investigations; depends on presentation and concerning features: recurrent palsy, neck mass, history of trauma

children.label: Acute otitis media with facial palsy
children: Doctor's note: AOM associated with facial nerve palsy: treatment includes antibiotics and pressure relief
Doctor's note: surgical intervention may be required to drain pus and relieve pressure on the facial nerve
Normal TM: pearly grey, neutral position, open Eustachian tube
AOM: purulent fluid, bulging TM, blocked Eustachian tube
Child with AOM-associated facial nerve palsy shows asymmetry when crying

children.label: Temporal bone fractures
children: Three types: oblique, longitudinal, transverse; some classifications describe only two main types: longitudinal and transverse
Longitudinal fracture: most common type; usually runs parallel to long axis of petrous temporal bone; facial nerve palsy less common
Transverse fracture: more commonly associated with facial nerve palsy than longitudinal fractures
Management, longitudinal: if facial palsy occurs, bleeding or haematoma may contribute to nerve compression
Management, longitudinal: if haemotympanum (blood in middle ear) present, assess pressure-related complications
Management, longitudinal: steroids alone may not be sufficient in significant nerve compression; depends on clinical findings
Management, transverse: assess location and extent of fracture and whether there is actual facial nerve injury
Management, transverse: if injury suspected → further evaluation and possible surgical exploration or decompression; coordinate with neurosurgery team when indicated

children.label: Parotid gland malignancy
children: Presentation: left upper neck swelling, protrusion of the lower auricle, facial nerve palsy
Diagnosis: MRI assesses parotid mass, its soft-tissue characteristics and suspected malignancy; biopsy confirms the diagnosis
Treatment: if malignancy suspected, may involve total parotidectomy, depending on extent of tumour
Benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma: superficial parotidectomy may be performed depending on location
Facial nerve runs through the gland, separating superficial and deep lobes; must be identified and preserved whenever possible
If palsy already present due to malignancy, nerve may be involved by tumour, affecting surgical management
Steroids are not definitive treatment for parotid malignancy
Imaging: trauma → CT (bony injuries); parotid mass → MRI (detailed soft-tissue assessment)

children.label: Peripheral vs central facial weakness
children: Peripheral (LMN): ipsilateral weakness of forehead, eye closure and lower face
Central (UMN): contralateral lower facial weakness with relative forehead sparing; this is not absolute
Clinical pearl: sudden facial weakness with arm/leg weakness, speech difficulty, diplopia, severe imbalance or other focal signs → activate Emergency Stroke Assessment
Clinical pearl: do not label every acute facial droop as Bell's palsy

children.label: Bell's palsy: definition and presentation
children: Acute, idiopathic, unilateral LMN facial nerve palsy; a diagnosis of exclusion
Typically reaches maximum weakness within 72 hours
Symptoms: facial asymmetry, inability to close eye, drooling, altered taste, sound sensitivity, peri-auricular pain, tearing changes
May involve forehead, eyelid and mouth on the same side
Typical cases diagnosed clinically; routine imaging/laboratory testing not needed unless features atypical

children.label: Bell's palsy: initial assessment and red flags
children: Document: onset/time, progression, prior episodes, vesicles/ear pain, hearing/vestibular symptoms, trauma, tick exposure/travel, cancer history, other neurologic symptoms
Examine facial movement at rest and with effort, grade severity, assess corneal protection and hearing/ear canal

Red flags: gradual progression, recurrent ipsilateral palsy, bilateral palsy, other cranial neuropathies, limb or speech symptoms, parotid/neck mass, vesicles, otitis/mastoiditis, no improvement as expected
Urgent evaluation: stroke features, corneal injury, severe infection, or rapidly progressive atypical weakness

children.label: Bell's palsy: treatment
children: Oral corticosteroid as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours, if no contraindication
Common adult regimen: prednisolone/prednisone ≈ 50–60 mg daily for 5 days followed by a 5-day taper, or accepted local equivalent protocol
Antiviral alone is not recommended
Consider adding valaciclovir/acyclovir in severe or complete palsy, after discussing uncertain incremental benefit
Protect the eye whenever closure is incomplete: frequent artificial tears by day, lubricating ointment at night, taping/moisture chamber during sleep
Review contraindications, comorbidities, pregnancy status, drug interactions and local guidance
Doctor's note: prednisolone 1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg
Doctor's note: tapering regimen = gradually reducing steroid dose rather than stopping abruptly
Doctor's note: eye care is very important in facial palsy, especially when patient cannot close eye completely
Doctor's note: physiotherapy and occupational therapy usually started after 2–6 months

children.label: Bell's palsy: follow-up and recovery
children: Many patients improve over weeks and continue recovering over months; recovery is variable
Reassess early: eye protection, diagnosis, adverse effects and progression
Urgent reassessment for new/worsening neurologic findings or ocular symptoms
Refer to ENT / Neurology / Facial Nerve Service if atypical, severe complete paralysis, or incomplete recovery around 3 months
Persistent sequelae: synkinesis, contracture, facial tightness, crocodile tears, residual weakness → consider facial neuromuscular retraining and specialist options

children.label: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus)
children: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) involving geniculate ganglion / facial nerve
Classic triad: 1) ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy, 2) severe otalgia, 3) vesicles on pinna/external auditory canal
Vesicles may appear later or be absent, called Zoster Sine Herpete (ZSH)
May include: hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, taste change and other cranial neuropathies
Inspect: pinna, concha, canal, tympanic membrane, palate and tongue; document hearing and vestibular symptoms
Often has poorer facial nerve prognosis than uncomplicated Bell's palsy
Doctor's note: clinical presentation: 1) facial nerve palsy; 2) skin eruptions around the ear; 3) vesicular eruptions involving the hard palate; 4) severe ear pain
Doctor's note: herpes zoster oticus = herpes zoster infection of ear region with vesicular eruptions around the ear

Doctor's note: Ramsay Hunt = reactivation of VZV involving geniculate ganglion, causing ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy and vesicular eruptions around ear or in oral cavity; other cranial nerves may be involved (particularly CN VIII)

children.label: Ramsay Hunt: treatment and precautions
children: Start antiviral therapy promptly: commonly valaciclovir 1 g orally three times daily for 7 days, or acyclovir/famciclovir per local guidance and renal function
Add a systemic corticosteroid when appropriate, commonly alongside the antiviral; assess contraindications and individual risk
Eye protection is essential if eyelid closure is impaired
Provide analgesia, assess hearing/vertigo, arrange ENT/audiology follow-up when indicated
Severe disease, immunocompromise, disseminated zoster, ocular involvement, multiple cranial neuropathies → may require urgent specialist/hospital assessment

children.label: Investigations: when are they needed?
children: Typical first-episode Bell's palsy: no routine imaging or laboratory tests
MRI with contrast for: gradual progression, recurrence, multiple cranial neuropathies, suspected neoplasm, or failure to recover
High-resolution CT temporal bone for: trauma or suspected bony/ear disease
Targeted testing guided by history/examination, e.g. Lyme serology, glucose/HbA1c, HIV or inflammatory tests when appropriate
Electrodiagnostic testing may help prognosis in severe/complete paralysis; timing and interpretation are specialist-led

children.label: Electrophysiological tests (ENoG and EMG)
children: Doctor's note: electrophysiological tests assess facial nerve function and muscle activity, help predict prognosis and guide management
Doctor's note: Electroneuronography (ENoG): usually done during first 14 days after onset of complete paralysis; assesses degree of nerve degeneration and predicts recovery
Doctor's note: ENoG results expressed as percentage of degeneration compared with unaffected side
Doctor's note: Electromyography (EMG): assesses electrical activity in facial muscles; determines whether voluntary motor activity is present; used alongside ENoG to guide management
ENoG < 90% degeneration: generally better prognosis and higher chance of recovery
ENoG > 90% degeneration: poorer prognosis, particularly if EMG shows no voluntary motor unit potentials
Doctor's note: in selected patients with complete paralysis, > 90% degeneration on ENoG and absent voluntary activity on EMG within 14 days, surgical facial nerve decompression may be considered
Doctor's note: decision depends on clinical situation and specialist assessment; ENoG result alone does not determine need for surgery

children.label: Other important causes: diagnosis-led management
children: Acute otitis media / mastoiditis: treat infection; urgent ENT assessment if complications or facial palsy
Lyme disease (endemic/exposure settings): test based on history and local guidance; treat with appropriate antibiotics
Temporal bone trauma: high-resolution CT when indicated, document onset and degree, urgent ENT and neurotology management
Parotid / skull-base tumour or facial nerve schwannoma: progressive or recurrent palsy, pain, mass, or multiple cranial nerves → MRI/CT and specialist referral
Stroke / brainstem lesion: emergency stroke/neuro pathway
Diabetes, sarcoidosis, HIV, Guillain–Barré (systemic): investigate and treat the underlying disorder

children.label: Complications and rehabilitation
children: Exposure keratopathy (corneal abrasion, ulceration, vision loss): prevent with eye lubrication and closure protection
Synkinesis (involuntary movement with voluntary movement): may benefit from facial neuromuscular retraining and botulinum toxin by experienced clinicians
Other complications: contracture, asymmetry, oral incompetence, speech/eating difficulties, psychosocial distress
Persistent weakness: facial nerve clinic, ophthalmology if eye risk, rehabilitation and selected reanimation procedures
Electrical stimulation is not routine first-line treatment; use evidence-informed specialist advice

children.label: House–Brackmann grading system
children: Classifies facial nerve palsy into six grades, from Grade I (normal function) to Grade VI (total paralysis)
Grade I, normal: normal function in all facial areas
Grade II, mild dysfunction: slight weakness on close inspection; complete eye closure with minimal effort; slight asymmetry with maximal effort
Grade III, moderate dysfunction: obvious but not disfiguring asymmetry; complete eye closure with maximum effort; reduced forehead movement
Grade IV, moderately severe: obvious weakness/disfiguring asymmetry; incomplete eye closure; no forehead movement
Grade V, severe: barely perceptible movement, marked asymmetry at rest, incomplete eye closure
Grade VI, total paralysis: no movement
Grade the whole face at rest and during movement; document side and date to track change; use the same scale at each visit
House–Brackmann is widely used; Sunnybrook offers more granular assessment of resting symmetry, movement and synkinesis
Severe/complete palsy warrants careful eye care and consideration of specialist assessment

children.label: House–Brackmann: doctor's notes
children: Doctor's note: Grade II vs Grade III is the most difficult distinction
Doctor's note: Grade II = good forehead movement and complete eye closure without effort
Doctor's note: Grade III = reduced forehead movement and complete eye closure only with maximum effort
Doctor's note: can facial nerve palsy be bilateral? Yes, it can affect both sides; bilateral involvement is less typical, so patient needs assessment for an underlying cause
